Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) for his observance of that parliamentary courtesy.
I have seldom given titles to speeches which I deliver in this place, but because of the issue before us, I thought that in this instance I would entitle my speech: "Living in Never-never-land with the Grits"; and it might have the subtitle: "Neither a borrower nor a lender be", the purpose perhaps being to advance a short course on what is involved in this borrowing authority Bill.
All of us in this House have listened with keen attention, not to say bated breath, to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) on the subject of guidelines. There has been nothing like it since "Goldilocks and the Three Bears", or was it the "Three Little Pigs"? If he erred on the side of naivete, or something else in that episode, he was quite sensible and down to earth in committee when in May the Minister said, and I quote:
I would not expect the House to act upon an additional request for borrowing authority without providing it with detailed information on the economic situation-
That is what he said, "detailed information on the economic situation in the form of a budget".
When you are talking in terms of $14 billion for a fiscal year which is not yet upon us and for which a budget has not yet been presented, nothing else surely will do. There must be a detailed financial statement with, as the Deputy Prime Minister has said, the implications of that situation on the Government's fiscal situation. That can only mean a budget.
It may come as a surprise to Members on the Government side, some of those on the backbenches, to be reminded, as seems to be an increasing requirement these days, that they are responsible to Parliament. They cannot come in here and get a blank cheque covering the next fiscal period without producing a budget which constitutes an outline of their fiscal and monetary position.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH

The borrowing authority demanded in the Bill constitutes an immediate inflationary pressure. It will force interest rates up, the most damaging development in the economy at the present time. We have had no indication from the Government of the purposes to which this enormous borrowing power will be put. It indicates an expectation of a deficit in 1983-84 considerably higher than the proposed $27 billion. Without a budget we have no indication of what policies this Government intends to implement to restore confidence, stimulate the economy and provide jobs.
Now the chickens are coming home to roost. This Government is faced with a major, almost disastrous, economic crisis. One cannot help being reminded of the fable by La Fontaine:
La cigale et la fourmi
"La cigale ayant chante tout Pete
Se trouva fort depourvue quand la bise fut venue."
I hope my accent was understandable.

To the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), I say "Go to the ant, thou sluggard", a piece of advice they would do well to embrace. Having brought the country to the sharp edge of insolvency, they want money. Without a budget, with no budgetary measures, no setting out of fiscal or monetary policy, they simply came into the House and said: "Fork over, boys", to the tune of $14 billion.
When one contemplates the financial situation of this Government, one is overcome with amazement that in a mere

three years so much could have been undone. It is a subject for students of political science and human conduct in years to come to attempt to explain how a Government could come down so fast, so far, in so short a time. What we must all be concerned about is that in its slide into insolvency and economic disarray, the Government has brought the entire economy down with it.
I, sir, am concerned about the size and the amount of this demand imposed on an already staggering economy in this country. It is conclusive proof, I submit, if any were needed at all, that this Government has no intention of mending its ways at all. Like a drunken sailor, it will go on throwing public money away until it leads this country to the edge of bankruptcy. The course of spending followed by this Government has been described as profligate, as wasteful and as reckless. It now, sir, borders on the edge of lunacy.
The first part of the Bill covering borrowing authority for $5 billion, representing part of the Government's cash requirements for the current fiscal year, must be taken in conjunction with the October budget. It is here that the details are set out covering the cash requirements for the current fiscal year. There are no such detailed explanations covering the second and larger amount of $14 billion.
As the Minister framed his demand, he must have been thinking of the lines from "The Ancient Mariner":
We were the first that ever burst
Into that silent sea.
It is a parliamentary first, sir, when you have a Minister who comes before Parliament and asks for authority to go to the public for $14 billion without the supporting and buttressing evidence of a budget. Perhaps he was thinking of the wreckage of the last three budgets now piled up on the beach. He decided to take the cash and let the explanations go until a later date. This House has been given no supporting documents, no financial picture, on the state of the economy, no current outline of fiscal and monetary policy. This mess which we are in is a direct result of mismanagement on the part of this Government. It is due to the two years in which the Prime Minister dragged the Canadian people through the labyrinth of constitutional reform. It is due to the Government's preoccupation with experimentation and centralization, and vast development programs which never got off the drawing board.
Giving this Government power to borrow $14 billion for unspecified purposes to be outlined in a budget which we have never seen is like giving a keg of whiskey to a drunk. This Government has a record of fiscal madness which is second to none. You have to go back, sir, to the Manchu dynasty to find a governing Party so remote from the ordinary citizens of this country.

speechtext:
Talk about the cart before the horse! This borrowing Bill is more evidence of the Government's mismanagement of the finances of the country. Its budgetary performance has been so inept that, in order to get one budget accepted by the House, it has to take three runs at it. We are now
working on a budgetary resolution covering three budgets, approving budgetary measures which should have been through this House months and months ago. Now this lethargic, incompetent aggregation of political misfits find themselves confronted by the necessity of producing another budget to cover current and upcoming demands, and they cannot do so until they get rid of the logjam of previous budgetary resolutions which have remained piled up in the House while they played with Canagrex and other non-essentials.
So what do they do? Do they follow normal procedure and bring in a budget, followed by a request for borrowing authority for the purposes spelled out in such a budget? Not at all. The Liberals have decided to cut the Gordian knot of their own incompetence by dispensing with the need for a budget and simply demanding the right to go into the market for their cash needs. First comes the cash, and then whenever they get around to it they will produce a budget justifying their demands for the cash.
We have had a bellyful of this Government cutting corners, bypassing Parliament, raiding the Treasury and attempting to govern without responsibility. It produced two unworkable budgets and a third which was simply an exercise in plastic surgery. It wandered away in a jungle of hazy schemes like the CIDC, the CDC, the NEP and FIRA, which consumed enormous amounts of money, involving, for example, the purchase of Fina and BP. Now that it is time to do its housekeeping, it is completely at a loss.
The Minister's desire to be orderly and efficient cannot be used as an excuse to deprive Parliament of its right to full explanations and respect for the traditions of this place. If the Minister and the Government are faced with meeting huge debt commitments and refinancing requirements, all we can say, in all bluntness, is: "Don't come crying on our shoulders". For years we have warned about the runaway expenditures of the Government, and for just as many years we have been totally ignored. When the day comes that the Liberals can walk into this House and demand permission to borrow $14 billion without any explanation, without detailed taxation measures and fiscal proposals outlined in a budget, then this House has no further function but to act as a rubber stamp for the demands of Government.

Here is a Minister who comes in after three disastrous budgets, with the economy on its beam ends, and says: "Let us not worry about a budget this time. Surely no finance company would lend money on those terms. What would be the collateral? A bunch of gas
stations?
Mr. Speaker, you, as the chief officer of Parliament, the guardian of its rights and privileges, the watchdog of its traditions, must be concerned about this abrogation of practice and tradition. You must surely be uneasy about a Government which comes in with all the finesse of Jack the Ripper and says: "give us money". Everyone who knows and respects Parliament and is aware of what this institution stands for must be conscious of the fact that if we sit still at this kind of hijacking of our rights, the institution itself will have entirely lost its validity.
We want the Minister to follow the practice of previous Ministers back to Confederation. We want him to outline his cash requirements for 1983-84 in a budget for that period, clearly outlining the state of the economy, the Government's fiscal and monetary position, the measures it contemplates taking to restore confidence and put Canadians back to work. That is the minimum that the Minister and the Government is obliged to accord Parliament. I warn the Minister and the Government, Parliament surely cannot stand for anything less than a full measure of its rights.
It would be the height of naivete to inquire why the Government tries so hard at every turn to evade parliamentary scrutiny. The Auditor General had something to say about that. He said the expenditures of the Government were entirely out of control. This latest demand by the Minister of Finance proves in spades that the Auditor General was exactly correct.
Parliament is being asked to underwrite expenditures for a fiscal year not yet begun, in reference to a budget which has not yet been presented. It is the Government's way of covering up the mess that it is in. It is a mess entirely of its own making.
For two years the Prime Minister, like a modern Moses, led the country through the desert of constitutional reform. He was not concerned about the economy, he was not concerned

about unemployment, he was not concerned about balancing the budget, he was not concerned about runaway deficits, he was not concerned about high interest rates, he was not concerned about accelerating bankruptcies, and he was not concerned about farm foreclosures.
None of that could penetrate the veil of mystical fanaticism in which he warpped himself. Like a prophet of old, he betook himself into a desert of his own making-with his "moozmaad"-and there he remained in isolation, fed by the ravens of his own party.
The problem which this country faces today, in spite of signs of an economic pickup in the United States, is that their policies have so disrupted the country's capacity to come back, that we may not get the benefit of their economic turn-around.
The Government is now in a position where it is borrowing to pay off its creditors. That is surely always a bad policy in financial circles. The request for authority to borrow $19 billion illustrates the chasm between the Government's perception of the economic parameters and the real needs of Canadians.
No one would object to a deficit, even one of the colossal proportions of the Government's deficit, if it meant that Canadians would get jobs. We know it will not mean that. It means a licence to the Government to continue its orgy of unproductive, ideological empire building. It means a licence to continue its ideological and destructive interventionism in the private sector. It means that this House is putting its seal of approval on policies which have driven this country to distraction, made us a laughing stock internationally, put hundreds of thousands of Canadians on the streets, and brought the economy to a rockbottom low. A deficit of this size creates a logjam in capital markets and reinitiates the battle over scarce capital that will result inevitably in pushing up interest rates.
The simple fact is that the resources the Government is asking for will not go to stimulating the economy. After all, it has had more than two years of the highest deficits and highest spending in the country's history to stimulate the economy. Instead, we have unemployment and foreclosures. So to suggest that this idiot Government is capable of providing jobs is to suggest that blood can be obtained from a stone.
There will be no new jobs, no stimulus. There will just be an added burden on the dead weight of centralist interventionism by the Prime Minister and his associates-both past and present-that will result in blocking our economy from benefiting from the resurgence now under way in the United States. They will use this to build an isolationist and separatist wall around the Canadian economy so that the benefits of the American comeback will not cross the border. That has been the record, and there is no warrant for believing that it will be anything different. There will be no end to the Liberal-induced recession in the country until the Liberal Government is removed from office.

Certainly a deficit would be permissible in normal times for a normal Government to attempt to stimulate the economy. A deficit of this size for a Government which has been spending like drunken sailors for more than two years on non-productive, self-defeating projects is simply not acceptable or permissible. This Government ought to be cutting out unrealistic and counter-productive expenditures, such as the incredible purchase of hundreds of gas stations which have become a drug on the market.
They could open doors and allow constructively-motivated investment to flow back into Canada and provide new jobs. They could back out of energy and allow the energy industry to operate in accordance with the realities of the day rather than the textbook fumbling of the Government. They could do these things, but they will not because the Government is as remote from reality as though it were on hashish. Nowhere in the Government is there any sign of repentance, regret or remorse.
They have run up the largest deficit in history, with the highest expenditures in history, yet they sit over there, proud of their dismal record. Rather than curtailing their own expenditures, they turned to the pensioners, the superannuates and public servants. Now, by demanding a lump sum advance payment of $14 billion, they evade the problem of coming before Parliament with specific budgetary measures in support of their demand for cash.
The other day the Minister rose in the House and went through the motions of explaining the need for $14 billion for the next fiscal year. This is what it amounted to. He said: "We are broke. We need money; $14 billion will do for now. If we need more-and we will-we will be back." He went on to say that the required explanations will be forthcoming in the budget which is forthcoming. As to the precise time when the budget would appear, he was vague. He said, of course, that we could turn to the "Economic Outlook" for further information. That too will be reviewed in the budget, not yet here but forthcoming. This is why the House must not agree to this Bill, without the necessary explanations and taxation measures clearly spelled out in a budget for the 1983-84 fiscal period.
The Minister expressed a desire not to be hindered by borrowing authority constraints. Surely in view of the record of the Government, it is a primary requirement that the Government shall be hindered in every way by constraints. That is precisely what we are here for-we are here to protect the interests of Canadians, not to see the country ripped off by the Government.

speechtext:
The real reason the budget has not been brought down to this point in time, to my mind, is that the economic situation, as I have stated, is changing very rapidly. If the Government were to bring down a budget which did respond to these very real, changing economic conditions, the Opposition would be the first group to howl that the Government was not forecasting properly, that the Government had done something improper in bringing down a budget before the Government really knew what the economic situation was. Changes are happening very fast. Changes are occurring very fast in this country and very fast in other countries. This affects our economic condition very dramatically. Economic change and economic recovery is coming about very quickly in the United States. That will have an impact upon employment in the primary Canadian industries. What kinds of programs should be in place in a budget will depend on where the areas of greatest need are in this country in light of the changing economic circumstances.
We will have the Estimates today at three o'clock. Given that the Minister has indicated his intense desire to bring down a budget at the earliest possible date, the Opposition will certainly have sufficient material to evaluate how the Government intends to spend the money it is asking for in this borrowing authority Bill.
Along the lines of the Bill itself and in trying to add something to the debate in this area, I would like to carry on with the comments I was making last Friday in the debate. I had to shorten my comments because another Hon. Member wanted to speak and we had to cut the debate short. At that time I indicated that the economic situation we faced in this country is no different in substance from the economic situation that is being faced by most, if not all, western industrialized countries. Certainly there are differences in the numbers as far as the unemployed in this country are concerned versus the numbers of unemployed in other countries. There is a difference in the level of inflation in this country versus other countries as well as differences in the level of interest rates and so on. But uniformly all countries are facing the same dramatically difficult economic situation.
The particular economic situation which faces the world has been in the making for a great many years. First it was in the form of inflation, and subsequently there were the attempts to bring that inflation under control made by all Governments.
It is important that we understand the nature of inflation and what must be done in order to bring inflation under control. Then we can argue whether or not Members in this House believe it is important that we bring inflation under control. If what causes inflation and what needs to be done to bring inflation under control is understood, then we can ask the question: Is fighting inflation worth the price? I suggest to
Borrowing Authority
you, Mr. Speaker, that it is worth the price. Indeed, there is no option but to bring inflation down.
Quite frankly, we have succeeded quite dramatically in the last year in bringing down inflation. If you look at the inflation rate on an annualized basis for the last three months, Mr. Speaker, you will find inflation is now running at 3.2 per cent. Similarly, if you look at inflation for the last six months, it is running at less than 6 per cent. That is a clear indication of the trend, the elimination of inflation which will lead to lower interest rates. All observers who have the slightest knowledge of economics understand that lower interest rates will be the key to stimulating the recovery of the economy.
Let me go back to inflation, Mr. Speaker. I believe the fight against inflation and the recession have very common characteristics. First with regard to inflation, inflation comes about as a result of a situation where the purchasing power in a system exceeds the output of the system. In other words, standards of living in a country can only rise as fast as productivity or the increase in output of the system. If the money supply, the purchasing power of the system, grows faster, it will lead to rising prices. There is no argument about that; it is a basic fact. That is what gave rise to the inflationary spiral we saw, which the United States saw, which western Europe saw and which all countries in the western world saw during the 1970s.
Can inflation be allowed to continue and be left to run on its own? The answer from the Opposition, the answer from the Government and the answer from other Governments in other countries has really been no. There are very good reasons why that answer was resoundingly no. Because inflation leads to increased uncertainty, it cuts back on investment. Without investment there is no growth. Without growth there are no rising standards of living. The situation leads to higher interest rates. This we saw in an all too real way during the 1970s and especially during the first part of the 1980s. That is the reason that we had to bring inflation under control. All Members in the House were very concerned about inflation and called upon the Government to bring inflation under control.
How does one bring inflation under control if it is growing because of the increase in purchasing power at a rate that is higher than the rate of output in the country? The only way to reduce inflation is to reduce the purchasing power so that it is back in line with output. If that is not done, inflation will not be brought down. High inflation means that our dollar income had been growing faster than the output of products that those incomes were to buy. Therefore, to reduce inflation incomes must be constrained in dollar terms.
What is inflation, after all, but the market's natural adjustment mechanism which tells an economic society that it has been living beyond its means? That is what inflation is, a sign that the market is adjusting for excess purchasing power through a reduction of incomes to reduce the purchasing power. In order to eliminate inflation, the growth of income

Borrowing Authority
has to be restrained so that it more closely corresponds to the growth of output.
The issue, then, is how should the income reduction in the system be distributed? In a normal, functioning marketing economy all individuals in society would share that reduction by some small amount. Unfortunately, that is not how our system or other systems in the western world operate. While the Japanese system operates that way to a much greater extent, our system operates on the basis that the great majority of people are able to protect their incomes and hold them at the previous level while the minority are deprived of incomes altogether. In other words, instead of our system adjusting to the fight against inflation by reducing everyone's income to bring income into line with output, it reduces the incomes of a few by a great amount and the incomes of many by very little. In other words, we throw people out of work rather than reducing incomes uniformly. The labour-management system in our country leads to that situation. Those who continue to be employed do very well but there are a large number of people who are thrown into destitution.
That is the system which has evolved in this country, in the United States and Western Europe over many generations. It is not a system that was introduced by this or any previous Government. Given this situation and the necessity to reduce inflation for all the reasons I have suggested, what can the Government do to raise our standard of living? There are methods which the Government can use. The Government can respond by reducing income security programs. The Government has done this over the years. We introduced the Unemployment Insurance Program to ensure that those people who are out of work as a result of this system have some kind of income to support themselves. We introduced welfare programs, medicare and public pension schemes.
If the system were to adjust normally, everyone's income would come down a little and employment would stay very high. This is the case in Japan where they have a 2.5 per cent rate of unemployment as opposed to our 12.5 per cent. In our system, however, a few are asked to take an enormous income loss while the rest have no income loss. The Government can respond by introducing programs and it can pay for those programs by imposing some form of involuntary tax, in the broad sense of the word, on those who continue to be employed in order to pay for those who are no longer employed. I believe that system is inefficient. Our compensation system should be modified and revised so that we have a more automatic, uniform and just method of adjusting to these changes which occur in our economy over a period of time.
There are three ways the system can pay for these kinds of income transfers. The first method involves the natural process of adjustment that comes about with inflation. Inflation effectively taxes people's incomes by raising prices and that inflationary system is generated by the increase in purchasing power. The increase in purchasing power is caused by increases in the money supply which is under the control of the Government. If the Government increases the money supply very rapidly and uses those funds to give money to people who are
out of work while generating inflation, it can pay for those programs in that way. However, we know that this is not a very efficient method because it will have a negative impact on future growth rates and standards of living. In fact, Governments all over the world have tried to stop that kind of process.
The second method which can be used is for the Government simply to tax those who continue to receive income and use those revenues for its expenditure programs that pay those who no longer have incomes. We are presently in a very deep and difficult recession. Any tax increase at this point could, and I believe would, lead to a much more severe recessionary situation than we now face. I personally believe that this is certainly not the time to be talking about any kind of direct tax increase.
The third method is effectively to borrow against the future, since taxes cannot be imposed today due to the very fragile economy. Therefore, these income support programs that are very necessary-which I believe no Member would deny- would be paid for through another form of tax called a deficit. A deficit is no more and no less than an increase in future tax liabilities. The present economic situation being as it is, I believe the best way to stimulate the economy and maintain the income support programs that are necessary in our economy is to use the deficit. In other words, borrow against the future to ensure that we establish the conditions for growth today. Through growth, we will be able to reduce the deficit in the future.
Let me say that there are some conditions which should be met. If the decisions were up to me, there would be certain conditions that I would place on that deficit, its nature and how it should be employed. First, I think the use of borrowed moneys from the increased deficit should be oriented wherever possible toward expenditures which are in the form of an investment in future growth. This could be in the form of public works programs, railway expansions, port development or other programs that improve the infrastructure of the economy and make it more efficient and lively in the future. It can be used in other areas, such as skill training programs which are an investment in human capital as opposed to physical capital. If the deficit is used to improve the lot of those who are out of work and are suffering from the recession in order to make them more capable of participating in the future growth of the economy and being able to have higher incomes than they had without the skill training program, then it is a very valid use of the money.
Of course, the money should be used for straight income support programs to ensure that the critical mass of skilled workers in adversely affected industries, such as the forest and mining industries, can remain in those jobs, when we know that the demand for those products will increase in the future. That critical mass of skilled people has to be maintained in these areas so the industry can rebound when the recovery comes.
I think the NEED Program is another area where the deficit can be used effectively with regard to employment. It is
February 22, 1983

designed to keep that critical mass of employment available as the recovery comes.
We could bring forward, of course, viable projects for immediate start in the private sector. The deficit could be used to finance programs which would help bring forward some of these programs which the private sector has delayed.
We could also, and most importantly-and we talked about this last week-invest more heavily in the expansion and development of research and development facilities and people in this country, which again is an investment in the future. It is an expenditure today but it is an investment in the future. All of these things will lead to a more robust recovery and allow us to handle the deficit more carefully.
As a final point, Mr. Speaker, all of us are concerned about the deficit. It is very large. It certainly can be justified on the basis of the kinds of reductions in income or reductions in tax revenue that the Government is faced with and the increase in expenditures for these income support programs that are very necessary. That is what is causing the deficit to go up.
In closing, I have to say that I would call upon the Government to ensure that in the coming budget a program for deficit reduction is clearly spelled out, so that Canadians know as the economy recovers, as the growth occurs, that the very high deficit that we have today will be reduced in a systematic manner over the next three to five to seven years, to a level in relation to GNP that we consider appropriate for long-term stability in the Canadian economy.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's figures mask a great many things. One is that we have had a very serious bout of inflation over the period of time and $12 billion in 1968 cannot be directly compared to $90 billion in 1983. We have had 15 years during which there has been some very serious inflation and as a result those figures would have to be deflated dramatically.
The second point is that there has been a dramatic increase and improvement in services that are provided by Government to Canadians. If you look at the expenditures of the federal budget, 50 per cent goes in transfers to Provinces and people in this country for services that are directly received by Canadians. Right now 25 per cent goes to servicing the interest on the public debt. That is one of the reasons inflation had to be brought down, to bring down the interest rate and reduce that proportion. The other 25 per cent is used for all other matters, including 10 to 12 per cent for defence. Therefore, about 13 per cent of the federal budget goes to administer the operations of Government.
Many observers who recently have looked at the pattern of Government expenditures have found no evidence of runaway federal Government expenditures in the last five years. There has been restraint in the federal Government, not runaway expenditure increases. The increases have come in the form of statutory programs, the cost of administering the deficit due to higher interest rates and in other such areas. These are the two areas which led to the increase in programs which we deal with in the Estimates. They have not been out of control. They have not grown inordinately.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us today another in a long and horrendous catalogue of borrowing Bills which this Government has placed before us since the February, 1980 election. It is the fourth of its kind in eight months-$6.6 billion in June, 1982; $7 billion in July, 1982; and $4 billion in November, 1982. The Government now has the temerity to request us to grant them a blank cheque. I do not know how Canadians, including Members of Parliament, could possibly visualize $19 billion and the other billions we have been asked for over the last three years. How could anyone visualize what is involved in that amount of money? It takes considerably more imagination that I could bring to bear.
The Government has given no clear indication as to how it intends to use this $19 billion. A few moments ago the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Nielsen) suggested that it would be difficult for any borrower to get funds from a finance company, unless he believed the TV commercial "Never borrow money needlessly, but when you must"-for a vacation, third car, winter holiday or summer cottage. Perhaps that is the airy-fairy kind of thinking which this Government has. It has given no clear indication of the purpose of these funds.
Anyone attempting to borrow money is asked a number of questions. They are asked about their plans. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has given no indication as to what his plans are. He simply says: "trust us". With this Government's record of shenanigans over the last few months, why should we trust them with another $19 billion on top of the $6.6 billion, $7 billion and $4 billion of the past eight months?
A borrower is also asked about his credit rating. The lender wants to know how he measures up in terms of meeting financial commitments. I received a letter today which deals with a situation which I have raised in this House many times. It is perhaps on a smaller scale but it shows the abominable attitude this Government, its Departments and agencies have when it comes to meeting payroll commitments to its employees. The letter I received in the mail today is addressed "To whom it may concern". I am sure it was forwarded to cabinet ministers and officials as well as to Members of Parliament. I quote from the letter:
I am writing this letter on behalf of the participants of the Salmo Workers Employment Society. (Employment Bridging Assistance Program). The reason of this letter is to find out why so many of the participants in this project are not receiving bi-weekly UIC pay cheques-
When we owe the government money they expect it promptly or there is an interest penalty of some kind added on. Why then, when the Government owes us, can't we expect the same treatment from them?
February 22, 1983

That is a worth-while question, especially today.
We can't rely on this money that we've earned to pay our bills and the interest is starting to add up. If the Government was to pay the interest on these past due bills, they may realize the unfair treatment they give us.
We are doing this work because the country is in need of it and they are far behind. We trudge through deep snow, work through all kinds of weather, and climb mountainous terrain to thin and space trees, while regular UIC people sit at home in warmth and collect UIC benefits on time, while we suffer on these long delays on our UIC pay cheques. How would you like to do this type of work and not get paid on time for it? Some employees can't even afford to bring a lunch or drive their vehicle to work. Since Louisianna Pacific Canada Ltd. has been shut down in 1981 there has been very few jobs available in this area.
We appreciate the opportunity of being a member of the Employment Bridging Assistance Program. On this program we have received a great amount of training and experience in the forest industry. We have the feeling of some importance knowing that we are aiding our country in these poor economical times, but, it sure would be appreciated to have more support from the Government themselves as the Province is in need of this work being done and they are profiting by it. We would appreciate it very much for your attention on this matter.
Many of those involved with the sending of this letter do not have a great deal of education. However, they are willing to work for very little in order that they can be useful and make a contribution to society. Despite repeated urgings and having the various technical and other problems brought to their attention, the Government still has not devised a system whereby these people could be paid every two weeks. If an employer with that kind of reputation tried to borrow rather heavily from some agency, he would be looked at questioningly-
This letter does not talk about normal delays. There is a list of 18 employees attached to this letter. One is behind seven weeks, three are behind four weeks, the next two are so far behind they have lost track, three weeks, three weeks, four weeks, another inestimable number, four weeks, three weeks, four weeks, three weeks, three weeks, six weeks, three weeks and three weeks.
That is the record of this Government when it comes to paying its own employees, not to mention payments on other matters which are not normally covered by legislation in terms of the time in which those bills must be paid. God knows what it does when it is not required by law to make payments. And, of course, the federal Government is not required by law to make these payments either because the provincial Governments, in concert with it, have seen to it that the parts of provincial legislation which require payment of wages on time is excluded. So the Government has even bent the laws and the rules.
This is not the time, necessarily, to give a long catalogue of the ills of specific programs, but they are symptomatic of the inability of this Government to meet its financial commitments and of its faulty sense of priorities. How is it that the country has managed to pile up the terrible debt burden which it has over the past number of years? There are a multitude of reasons, Mr. Speaker, and Hon. Members are very aware of some of them. It is interesting to note that at a time when we are being asked to authorize the borrowing of another $19
Borrowing Authority
billion as of June, 1982, the cumulative total of deferred corporation taxes was some $20.8 billion. We in this Party believe that deferred taxes are actually interest-free forgivable loans given to corporations through the taxation system. That is money which is owed to the people of Canada and which has not been paid. It has been deferred for a number of reasons, but ordinary Canadians do not have the right to defer their taxes. It seems incumbent upon some of us to point this out at a time when we are being asked to authorize the borrowing of yet another $19 billion. The corporate sector is not asked, or has not been asked over a number of years, to pay those debts, and that means that the rest of Canadians must.
Just the other day I received a copy of "Beale's Letter", an independent newsletter which is generally sent to chief executive officers in the forest industry mostly in the Pacific Northwest, but actually right across the continent. The editor of the newsletter-and it is a highly regarded one within the forest industry-was in Tacoma, Washington recently, and in this particular issue he dwells on some comments of an industrialist in the Tacoma area. He quotes the industrialist as saying:
If there's one thing that really worries me about Canada today, it's political uncertainty. What's going to happen to Trudeau? Will he be around another 10 years? And as for Clark-when he was prime minister it seemed Canada had no government at all.

One of the major items which has led to the large deficit which we have today is the matter of deferred corporate taxes owing, the amount of which is almost equal to what is being asked for today. That general scheme of forgiven taxation is not only supported and advocated by the Government but has been supported strongly by the Official Opposition. The huge multi-billion dollar grants which were given to the oil and gas industry within the period of the last year was not only the

policy of the Government, but was supported by the Official Opposition. Huge bail-outs of the corporate sector have taken place, especially over the last few years, and hundreds of millions of dollars on each occasion has been taken out of the public purse. The public purse had been used continuously to bail out losers, and this has also been supported on both sides of the House.
What confidence can we, therefore, have when these holus-bolus hand-outs are given, either directly or by simply not collecting the money which the people are owed? How can we have confidence as long as it appears that one or the other of the two major Parties in this House, the Liberals or the Tories, will likely be the Government and this policy is not likely to be changed? How can we have any secure feeling whatsoever? We cannot.
There are two or three other programs which I would like to draw Hon. Members' attention to while discussing this Borrowing Authority Bill because they demonstrate again the incompetence of that bunch over there with their faulty sense of priorities. One such program is the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. Among so many of the Government's employment-creation programs, this has been one of the most popular and most long standing. There were problems with it in its infancy, but they have been largely resolved. It has a well established delivery system and is one of the most productive and job-intensive programs ever to be offered by the Government, producing some $3 in job-creating private housing expenditures for every $1 of Government funds expended. It has also in its social purpose contributed greatly to many senior citizens, particularly, and to many other Canadians of modest means, enabling them to retain their own homes, which is surely a worth-while social objective.
Yet at a time when our national unemployment rate is some 1.6 million officially, when British Columbia's rate is 16 per cent, we see the RRAP budget for the British Columbia-Yukon region being reduced by some 15 per cent. At this same moment the Government is bragging that it has increased the individual amount of forgivable loans from $3,700 to $5,000. It has reduced the total amount available and issued directives which really leave us with a feeling that the operative slogan of the Government now should be: "Let the user of Government programs beware". Its directives have been to the co-ordinators of this program in the various areas, telling them not to advise people of the forgivable loan aspects of the program, and to try only to lend money which will be repayable. one part of the country to be used in the program in other areas which have demonstrated a need. Again, those allocations have been included in the budget and have been provided. With a program of job creation which is as useful and beneficial as this one, why should the Government deprive those areas which have shown initiative and have the demonstrated need for housing and jobs? subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak in the debate on the borrowing authority Bill today because this is a very important request that the Government is making. It is a request from a Government that has no concept whatever of financial responsibility, no understanding of the trust placed in it by Canadians and no comprehension of the need to demonstrate a concern for spending control or restraint.
The Government of six and five is coming before us with a borrowing request for $19 billion-$5 billion this year, $2 billion to curry over to next year, plus another $14 billion- $16 billion for next year. That is the largest borrowing request in the history of this Parliament. The Government will probably require another $19 billion after the $16 billion is used up to carry it through the balance of the year. It has asked for a total of $26 billion to date and has clearly shown that it is a Government which is out of control.
Let us examine the record, Mr. Speaker. In November, 1981 in the infamous MacEachen budget, the deficit was estimated at $10.5 billion and the borrowing requirement was some $6.5 billion. Eight months later, in June, 1982, the deficit had
almost doubled to $19.5 billion and the borrowing requirement had gone up three times to about $17 billion.
Then we had a change of players. In September, 1982 we had a new Minister, one who would take control and would show that he knew what was going on. We heard that he would probably be a little more conservative in his estimates to show that he had things under control and would perhaps be able to cut back the borrowing requirement or the size of the deficit before the year was out. His first guess was that the deficit would be about $23.5 billion and the borrowing requirement would be $22 billion, an increase of $4 billion and $5 billion respectively over his predecessor's estimates.
Now we have the man who had it all under control telling us that the deficit is $27 billion, about 2.5 times the original estimate, and that the borrowing requirement is $26 billion, four times the original estimate. How could any Government be so far out in its estimates made just 15 months later? The utter contempt that this Government is showing Parliament and Canadians is unprecedented. In face of this incredible demonstration of incompetence, it is coming to Parliament and saying: "Give us a blank cheque. Give us a free rein over spending for the next few months. We are not going to tell you what is happening. We want total carte blanche to the end of this year before we come back, cap in hand, asking for more money."
There is no spending plan, no stated purpose for the amount of money required, no real control indicated of how the Government will keep its spending within reasonable limits. It is bad enough to be embarking on this crazy spending spree, but the Minister is breaking a clear commitment that he made to Parliament four or five months ago.
Last October the Minister said:
In the budget I intend to present early in 1983, I will review again the fiscal situation for the current fiscal year-
He has not done that.
-set out estimates for 1983-84-
We have not seen them.
-and future fiscal years-
We have not seen any since November, 1981.
-and then seek additional borrowing authority as required.
As my colleague the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Nielsen) just said, he is putting the cart before the horse and in so doing is breaking the clear commitment he made to Parliament in October, 1982. That fiscal plan must be presented to Parliament. That is why he is showing such contempt for Parliament and Canadians. There is no sense of need or of giving reasons why this borrowing authority is necessary today. That is why we oppose it so strongly.
This is quite consistent with what we have seen in the House in the past few days, Mr. Speaker. There is an utter lack of principle, an ignoring of guidelines on conflict of interest, as the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) told us yesterday. It is quite consistent with the ignoring of the principles
February 22, 1983

that have been established over the years on control of spending by Parliament.
Here is a Government with the Deputy Prime Minister sitting on a platform with a former minister, Mr. Gillespie, when he knew that the Government of Canada had to sign an agreement, when he knew that the former minister stood to make a gain of $725,000 personally, when he knew there were no tenders being called by the Government for this particular project. It did not cross his mind that he should question whether there was something being done that was contrary to the principles of this Parliament, contrary to the guidelines that had been established.
What did we get from him yesterday? He said that those guidelines are there to be broken, that the guidelines are there for the conscience of the Ministers themselves. But if the Ministers have no conscience and if the Ministers have no principles, those guidelines are not worth the paper they are written on. That, Mr. Speaker, is the sort of Government we have been receiving from these people for 15 years and it is a Government that must be changed.
Let us look at what the borrowing authority signals to Canadians today. It shows that the spending of the Government is totally out of control; but worse, it is showing Canadians that there is no real sense of concern about this, no sense of concern that there is any real intention of submitting itself to the normal constraints of Parliament. It is asking for a blank cheque.
Last October the Minister said it would not be right to request more borrowing authority until the budget was brought forward with a Five-year plan. Now, five months later, totally ignoring the principles he established at that time, he is saying; "Give me that blank cheque".
The last time we had a Five-year plan was in November, 1981. It was out of date before it was presented in the House of Commons. The Minister has not had the courtesy or the principle to set before the House a Five-year plan on which we as Canadians can judge where we are going and how we will get there before we give the Government approval to spend taxpayers' money. We have no idea of the budget deficit for next year. We have no idea of the financial requirements. We have no idea of the spending or the revenues which the Government has in mind for next year or the five-year period thereafter. Yet the Minister wants $19 billion of borrowing authority without any strings attached. It is essential that the Government honour the obligation made to the House and through the House to Canadians. We must have that commitment before we approve this Bill.
Interest rates during the last few months have been going up in the area of the marketplace which is established by the private investor, the saver, or people who have their money at risk. These are not the rates which are manipulated by the Bank of Canada; these rates are a reflection of the broad concerns in the marketplace at this time. These rates have been going up since the middle of December, but, more important, real interest rates or interest rates after the impact
Borrowing Authority
of inflation are at a near record high at this time. Last month inflation dropped one percentage point to about 8.3 per cent, which is down from about 12 per cent last summer. If we look at a more concentrated period of time, say the last six months, we will see that it ranged from 6 per cent to 6.5 per cent or, as the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) told us today, it is down to 3.2 per cent. That is his figure. I have not checked it out but I will take his word for it.
The reason Canadians are worried about the value of their money is very simple. They are worried that the dollars they have invested today in a Government bond or in a mortgage will lose their present value. This is why real interest rates after inflation are so high. Also they are concerned because they see that runaway budget deficits will lead to more inflation. Deficits also mean that Governments will borrow; Governments will go into the marketplace and compete with the private sector. That competition with the private sector will force up interest rates. It forces up the cost of money, which is interest rates. The federal Government will borrow some $30 billion this current calendar year, provincial Governments will borrow some $20 billion and the private sector will borrow another $20 billion. That combination must force up interest rates. It means that money invested today will be worth less some short period of time down the road.
Another reason for the fear is a lack of confidence over what the Government is doing. Let us look at what happened in 1981 and let me remind the House of that disastrous budget. We all know of its disastrous effects across the country. It hurt people who were small-businessmen, people who were on pensions, people who had health care plans, people who were trying to save for their retirement, farmers, Fishermen, people in the North and businesses in general. All these people were hurt by that budget.
Why did the then Minister of Finance attack these people? It was not because he had any outrageous desire to hurt them; that is not what a politician likes to do. He said: "I am broke; the Government is broke. We need money. We have to get some money in the till." The Government was desperate at that time. It knew the deficit was too high. It was worried about it, so it brought in that budget in an attempt to get more money through an increase in taxes on that wide range of people.
If there was a problem in the 1981 budget with the deficit projection, as I reminded the House a minute ago, of $10.5 billion, think of the problem today with budget deficits of some $26 billion. Next year we are hearing stories that it could be as high as $30 billion. What is that doing to people? What is that doing to Canadians who are wondering what will happen to them in the next budget? They are very concerned that the same attack will come through increased taxes, taxes which will take away their ability to grow. They see their ability as small businesses to grow and create jobs for people taken away. A huge deficit increases the pressure on the Minister of Finance to increase taxes and to remove tax incentives which lead to planned expansion, the development of new technology

February 22, 1983
Borrowing Authority
or the creation of jobs. This is why Canadians are worried today. This is what a high budget deficit means to them when we get down to the raw, real terms of the marketplace.
It is difficult to comprehend the runaway deficit. It is a huge amount of money. What is $27 billion? Can we picture how much money that is? It is very difficult to comprehend. This year with that deficit it means that each Canadian-every man, woman and child-will be going into debt by $1,125. Or to put it in family terms, in terms of our responsibilities as family people, it means that each family will be seeing its debt load through the Government of Canada increase by $3,700. That will be repeated next year, and it will be probably a little more because of a higher deficit that year. Whether it is in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, British Columbia, Manitoba or Ontario, it is all the same-we will see our debt load increase by $3,700 per family.
Let us get down to the hard facts. Let us look at the impact of this on job security, the competitive position of the companies for which we work, and their ability to stay in business and continue to provide the jobs we need. We are all aware of the drop in the value of the Canadian dollar over the past eight years. This is one clear indication of the loss of a competitive position in the country. We are all aware that the deficit in our manufacturing trade balance has increased over the past ten years from $3 billion to $20 billion. This is also an indication that we are losing our competitive position. We are all aware that Canada is last in productivity of the industrialized countries of the world. This is another reason we are losing our competitive position.
What does all this mean to the average Canadian? It means that jobs are being lost, companies are going bankrupt, and small businesses are in the most serious position they have been in the last 20 to 40 years. How do we get out of this mess? How do we break the downward spiral of the Canadian dollar? How do we regain the competitive position we have lost in the past few years? We have to do all we can to help small-businessmen and large-businessmen take the necessary steps to recover our competitive position on a broader industrial basis. This means that we must give them incentives to expand, to buy new machinery, to develop and acquire new technology, not just for the high technology, glamour companies of the world, but for run-of-the-mill companies which need that technology just to maintain their position in an international environment. The deficit to them means potentially higher taxes. It means that the cost of the money they will need to allow their companies to expand will increase because Governments are competing directly with them.
When the Government shows no indication through the borrowing requirement it puts before us that it has its deficit under control or that it has any serious resolve to bring it under control, when Canadians see the deficit increase 2.5 times in 15 months and the financial requirements of the Government four times in that same period, is there any wonder there is a lack of confidence in what the future holds for the country?
I have spoken about small businesses and other businesses, but the same applies to individual families. I said that real
interest rates, the interest rates after adjusting for inflation, are close to a record high today. We know that savings rates are high and that Canadians are putting record amounts of money into the sock for a rainy day. Why is that? With these record high interest rates it makes sense to save. If inflation is falling there is no urgency to rush out and buy that new car or that new stove because the price will be much higher in the next few months. It will not be higher because inflation rates are coming down. People are being encouraged to save.
Canadians are also worried because they feel they will lose their jobs. One million, six hundred thousand Canadians have lost their jobs, and if taxes are to increase because of high inflation, more jobs will be lost in the future. Canadians are taking the cautious course. They are taking a sensible course. They are leaving their money where it can be drawn upon for that rainy day.
I have shown why this deficit, this run away spending, is a fundamental problem for all Canadians. It is not just a number; it is a major threat to our way of life, our industrial base. It affects the ability of our industries to provide jobs for our economic future. By bringing in this totally irresponsible borrowing Bill the Government is showing no understanding of the problem, and by demonstrating this total lack of comprehension, it is making the problem far worse than it need be.
I urge the Government to adopt a three-part program for deficit control in its upcoming budget. This is absolutely essential if the Government is to face its loss of confidence out there among Canadians as a result of its policies.
Let me outline briefly what this three-point program is. First, we have to recognize that the safety net in place today cannot be changed. The safety net of Unemployment Insurance and welfare programs is there just for the times that we are now experiencing. Let us leave that safety net in place and recognize that there will be an increase in cost there.
Second, in order to finance that increased cost, the Government must review all Government spending programs, weed out the unproductive ones and either cancel them or defer them. That must be an objective in this forthcoming budget.
Third, I want to address the problem of the structural deficit, which has been growing from zero about ten years ago to $1 billion, $2 billion or $3 billion, then up to $5 billion, to a level of $10 billion for four years, and now it is over $20 billion. In fact, the deficit is close to $30 billion.
The Government must bring in a long-term plan to bring the structural problem under control. I do not want to hear any figures like those the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre brings in. He says that the deficit will drop down to about X billion dollars in five years' time. Those figures do not mean anything. We know that from experience over the last 15 months. However, we must see a program that brings this structural problem under control on a long-term basis.

I believe there is a broader problem that we face in the country today, above and beyond the short-term problem of the international recession. We have been trying to draw this to the attention of the Government over the last few months.
Let us stand back and look at some of these broader problems that are coming together at this point in time. There are four points that I wish to outline. First, over the past two or three years we have suffered a major regional conflict, East versus West. That causes problems right across the country.
Second, during the same period of time this Government in particular has provoked differences between Canada and our major trading partners. That problem and the effect it has on our ability to trade and on our ability to deal and reach agreement on some major problems with the United States is hurting our short-term economy.
Third is the problem of the over-all micro-technology revolution, the information revolution. We have not faced up to that in the way we should as a people, and certainly this Government has not been leading our thinking in that direction.
The fourth problem I lay directly in the lap of this Government, that of its over-all role. This Government opposite over the past three years has taken on far too much of a requirement to solve every problem. It has concentrated too much of the decision-making within the bureaucratic apparatus that is here in Ottawa rather than having trust in the people, whether they are small-business people or otherwise.
It is the confluence of those four major areas that is at the heart of why Canada is suffering so much from international

subtopic: RESPONSIBILITY ATTACHING TO PARLIAMENTARY IMMUNITY
RESPONSIBILITY ATTACHING TO PARLIAMENTARY IMMUNITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, immunity is a precious privilege conferred on parliamentarians so that they may better pursue the good of the state and of its citizens. However, like all privileges, the one of parliamentary immunity carries with it an awesome responsibility which is to ensure the protection of the innocent.
No court in the land would admit innuendo or unsubstantiated statements. No court in the land would deny or curtail the right to defence, whether the subject be a private citizen or a former Minister of the Crown.
Let this Parliament, then, as the highest court of all, pay extra heed to the responsibility of its Members lest, in the heat of debate and the glare of publicity, they besmirch innocent reputations, deny equal time and opportunity for rebuttal, and find themselves guilty of morally reprehensible character assassination.

subtopic: ONTARIO INDIAN FISHING AGREEMENT
ONTARIO INDIAN FISHING AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Ontario Indian Fishing Agreement is a matter of great concern to anglers, tourist operators and outfitters throughout the Province of Ontario.
This tripartite Agreement which has been signed by the Province of Ontario and native leaders, but has yet to be signed by the Government of Canada, calls for the granting of certain fishing privileges to the Indian people and the zoning of some lakes for a five-year period.
The lack of information provided to the public by the three parties negotiating the Agreement has resulted in concern and uncertainty among non-Indians throughout the Province. This is a direct result of the lack of public knowledge as to the purpose of the Agreement and the effects that it will have on fishing if and when it is implemented.
February 22, 1983

The controversy surrounding this Agreement is primarily due to a lack of public information and public input. As it appears that the federal Government is on the verge of signing this Agreement, I strongly urge that this Government and the other parties to the Agreement hold public information sessions across the Province, particularly in northern Ontario, to explain the Agreement and all its implications. In order to remove the suspicions that have resulted from misinformation and misrepresentation concerning the Agreement, these public information sessions are essential.
I urge the Government to ensure that allowance will be made for public input on this matter which is causing great, and perhaps unnecessary concern to many residents of the Province.

maintopic: CONTRACT FOR SALE OF EQUIPMENT TO CHILEAN PRISONS
CONTRACT FOR SALE OF EQUIPMENT TO CHILEAN PRISONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was dismayed to learn that the Canadian Government is now in the business of promoting the sale of security equipment for Chilean prisons. Only three months ago the United Nations Report on human rights in Chile stated that there has been a substantial increase in torture in that country. Torture is an habitual practice of Chilean security agencies which can legally detain people for up to 20 days before placing them in the hands of the courts.
Our Government's role in the sale of this equipment is distressing, not only because of the likelihood of Chilean prisoners being tortured but also because it is a clear violation of the Government's own position regarding the sale of such equipment to that country. On August 31, 1981, the then Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Hon. Mark MacGuigan, wrote:
-our own view is that defence equipment may be sold to Chile so long as that country is not involved in hostilities and Canadian equipment is not used against the civilian population.
But now a project officer from the Defence Programs Branch of External Affairs has been assigned to help five Canadian companies prepare their bids to sell military and security equipment to Chilie. The information that I have is that the equipment they are trying to sell includes an intrusion detection system for three new Chilean prisons. In addition, the Program for Export Market Development has approved a grant to one of these companies to help defray the costs of presenting the contract bids to the Chilean military government. The companies involved are planning to present their bids to the Chilean government this spring. I would urge the Government, instead of promoting the sale, to take immediate steps to stop it.

subtopic: ARREST OF DR. YOSIF BEGUN BY SOVIET AUTHORITIES

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: ARREST OF DR. YOSIF BEGUN BY SOVIET AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Dr. Yosif Begun, a Soviet Jew, who first applied to leave the U.S.S.R. in 1971, has been arrested and faces the possibility of a third term in prison. Dr. Begun has been convicted twice before, and since 1977 has served a two-year and a three-year prison term for trying to maintain his Jewish identity and to teach the Hebrew language.
On November 6, 1982, Dr. Begun was arrested and informed that he would be charged with anti-Soviet propaganda and agitation and face a 12-year sentence. His arrest came only five days prior to the scheduled opening of the Madrid Review Conference. This can only be interpreted as a direct provocation and denigration of the Final Act of the Helsinki Accords and the principles which Helsinki embodies. As such, it is an affront to Canada and the other signatory states.

subtopic: ELIMINATION OF JOBS IN NEW BRUNSWICK
ELIMINATION OF JOBS IN NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadian Pacific Railway facilities in New Brunswick have suffered substantial lay-offs in the past 16 months. Twenty-eight jobs have been lost from the customer service centre and 62 truckers were let go recently. Rumour threatens that another 17 jobs will be lost in Saint John and McAdam on May 1.
The CPR employees are appealing to the federal Government to assure them of protection and fair treatment. Clerical employees are suffering a $3,300 financial loss because of the six and five restraints, and continue to lose their jobs at an alarming rate. They are being squeezed from both sides.
The Brotherhood of Railway, Airline and Steamship Clerk locals in Saint John are asking the CPR to adopt policies of retirement at 55 with full pension, job reduction only through attrition, and the retention of all employees now holding permanent jobs. The adoption of these proposals would make it

February 22, 1983
possible for CPR employees to hold their jobs with confidence and security.
As the federal Government has regulated CPR to adhere to the restraint program, it carries the responsibility of assuring that the employees are offered some protection from unwanted job loss. On behalf of CPR employees I appeal to the Government to adopt these proposals and consider the significant ramifications of further lay-offs on both the employees and the region.

subtopic: VEGETABLE GREENHOUSE INDUSTRY-IMPACT OF ENERGY COSTS
VEGETABLE GREENHOUSE INDUSTRY-IMPACT OF ENERGY COSTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to draw attention to the threatened existence of the vegetable greenhouse industry due to the rising costs of production, one of the major components of which is energy in the form of natural gas.
In the early 1970s it was estimated that energy costs represented approximately 20 to 25 per cent of the greenhouse growers' operational costs. Today, due to increasing prices, energy costs represent at least 50 per cent of those production costs, and are rising.
These rapidly increasing costs have put the industry under extreme pressure because of the need for greenhouses to be built of uninsulated glass or plastic, to provide for sufficient light to ensure a good crop. This prerequisite has minimized the cost of efficient energy conservation opportunities which have been available to other industries over the same period. The problem the industry is experiencing is evidenced by the fact that stabilization payments were paid to the growers in all but one year since the 1977-79 growing season.
To alleviate this pressure, representatives of the Ontario Greenhouse Vegetable Growers' Marketing Board have met with the Government to request that the federal excise tax on natural gas, first introduced in 1980 and now equalling 68 cents per MCF, be refunded to those growers in food production.
I would add my support to this worthy proposal and urge the Government to act upon this request, by using the experience and mechanism of refunding the excise tax to other farmers in the production of food. This act of equity would help ensure that the greenhouse vegetable growers continue to operate-

subtopic: UNITED STATES REACTION TO ACID RAIN POLLUTION
UNITED STATES REACTION TO ACID RAIN POLLUTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to address the serious problem of continued Government inaction on the acid rain problem that threatens our lakes, forests, farmlands, and health. In a comprehensive report released yesterday, hand picked Reagan-supporting American scientists would not agree with Canadian scientists that current sulphur dioxide emissions should be cut in half. The American response has been to demand further studies, further reviews, and further inaction. That is a view created by the manipulative politics of Reaganism that put the interests and profits of industrial polluters before the health, well-being, and economy of the North American public.
When is the Minister of the Environment going to legislate acceptable limits to acid rain? When will he convene a lobby of Members of Parliament and scientists to address the U.S. Congress on acid rain and toxic waste dumps? When will the Prime Minister get involved to ensure an agreement with the United States is reached? When will the Government take unilateral action to stop these deadly emissions? When will the Government admit that the steps that it has taken to date have so far just promoted the status quo?

February 22, 1983

If the Liberal Government put as much enthusiasm into solving acid rain as it has into achieving a weapons testing agreement with the United States, we would have a solution. Instead, Canada is and will continue to be a waste dump for U.S. industry.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (President of Treasury Board):
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is the first step in Parliament's consideration of the detailed expenditure budget of the Government for 198384. It is for Parliament to grant final approval of this spending plan. When approved, these Estimates establish the framework within which the activities of the federal Government itself are carried out and accounted for. Tabling of these Estimates is the end of months of intensive preparation by the Government.

Madam Speaker, the Main Estimates provide a detailed and comprehensive description of the Government's present policies, activities and programs. However, they do not give more than an overview of total government spending as projected at the present time. If we consider the time required for decision-making and producing the forty-nine volumes that make up the Estimates this year, it means that the Federal Government must be able to adapt to the circumstances and have the flexibility to review and revise its programs so as to promote economic recovery.
Madam Speaker, I also wish to remind Hon. Members that the budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) expects to bring down shortly may very well affect the Government's expenditure plan for the coming year. Of course, any changes in the Estimates as a result of the budget will require approval by Parliament of Supplementary Estimates or a separate Bill. The Government's 6 and 5 program has also had an impact on the Estimates. Capping of compensation in the Federal Public Service and capping of Old Age Security benefits, family allowances and indexing of public service pensions has made funds available for creating jobs and establishing other programs to help Canadians cope with these difficult times and speed up the country's economic recovery.

This year the Estimates are presented as a group of volumes: Part I, The Government Expenditure Plan; Part II, the Estimates proper, long referred to as the Blue Book; and Part Ill's
Main Estimates, 1983-84
Program Expenditure Plans that provide detailed program information.
This is the third year Part I has been prepared and tabled. It provides Parliament with an overview of Government spending in a form conducive to an understanding of total expenditures, and focuses on the broad policy areas to which resources are allocated by Parliament through programs of Departments and agencies.
Part II, that is the Blue Book, continues to support the items that may eventually be included in the Appropriation Act, of the Main Estimates. When the new form of the Estimates is fully developed, there will be changes to the form and content of Part II. However, this year it is the traditional Blue Book in structure and content.
Several volumes of Part III are tabled this year for the second time and a further number are provided for the first time. These volumes, 47 in all, provide information to the Standing Committee of Parliament that has the task of examining the Estimates for each Ministry. Each volume includes explanations of what the Department expects to achieve with the resources requested and includes, where possible, a statement of the benefits expected from the program. Part III will be expanded over the next few years to include volumes for all Departments and agencies. Therefore I have tabled, on behalf of my colleagues, the 47 Department Expenditure Plans. These documents, which are prepared by and are the responsibility of individual Departments, provide a great deal of further detail on Government programs and, more specifically, what the Government hopes to achieve with the money it plans to spend through these Estimates.
In recognition of the fact that individual Members will have particularly strong interest in examining certain programs and Departments but not others, we are not having automatic distribution of all volumes of Part III to all Members. However, Members can obtain these documents from the Parliamentary Distribution Centre by simply indicating those of interest to them on a list of available volumes included with their copies of Part I and the Blue Book.
A further initiative in improving the information available to Parliament is the planned revision of the Blue Book. As I have said, the new concept of the Estimates calls for presentation in three parts. Because consultation with Members on the form of Part I and Part III proved very constructive, it is my intention to initiate in the near future discussions with Members on proposals to amend the form and content of the current Blue Book. I would only note at this time our expectation of a reduction in the volume of the Blue Book when all part III books are available and it becomes possible to relocate information to Part III without reducing the information available to Parliament for its consideration.
I would now like to focus on Part I of the Estimates, the Government Expenditure Plan. The updated plan for 1983-84 and the information related to 1982-83 reflect the policies and programs announced by the Ministers of Finance in the June,
