speechtext:
Even while funding substantial increases in existing and new measures to assist Canadians in this difficult economic period, the Government has been able to restrain over-all spending growth by implementing a number of spending restraint initiatives. The restraint program announced in the June budget, which, of course, directly affects about one-half of total spending, results in funds available for reallocation of over $700 million in wages and salaries, Old Age Security, Family Allowance payments and Public Service pension costs. In addition, planned spending on aid to developing countries and on defence was reduced by several hundred million dollars. Much of the over-all 9.6 per cent spending increase is due to programs designed to protect those Canadians most in need, to provide support to sectors hard hit by the recession and to enhance the prospects of economic recovery.
Within this total expenditure plan of $88.9 billion, these Main Estimates provide for budgetary expenditures of $85.6 billion, and for $1.8 billion in loans, investments and advances. Within the over-all plan the Government has $0.9 billion in reserves to cover adjustments to statutory programs as well as $2.4 billion in envelope reserves to cover cost adjustments to other programs and to provide for planned but not yet announced initiatives. I should emphasize that these reserves are not free money for which no use has been found. A substantial portion is simply a prudent contingency fund against the inevitable uncertainties of precisely anticipating thousands of costs over one year in advance.
In regard to remaining reserves, Government decisions and approvals in principle have already been developed which effectively earmark the reserves for a variety of initiatives. Once the details of such items are finalized, and should any of the contingency funds be required, parliamentary approval will, of course, be sought through Supplementary Estimates.
The planned total outlays of $88.9 billion also reflect two other adjustments. First, Estimates must be adjusted down by the forecast $0.5 billion in repayments on loans issued in previous years. Second, since the Government cannot legally spend more money than Parliament authorizes, and in fact always spends less, a downward adjustment for the lapse of expenditure authority must be made, for which the current projection is $1.4 billion.
I would now like to focus on the $85.6 billion in budgetary expenditures provided for in these Main Estimates. Thirteen items account for about 80 per cent of the total increase of $12.7 billion in budgetary Main Estimates. These items include increases of $2.7 billion in payments to persons for Old Age Security, Guaranteed Income Supplement, spouse's allowances and the Government's contribution to Unemployment Insurance benefits. Increases of $2.2 billion occur through transfers to the Provinces under the Established Programs Financing Program, the Canada Assistance Plan and fiscal transfer payments. Public debt costs are up $1.8 billion. Other items in this category are petroleum incentives payments, National Defence, direct job creation, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Trade Industrial Program of Industry, Trade and Commerce, payments to VIA Rail and the budget of the Canadian International Development Agency.

Although Hon. Members will find a host of explanations and information on changes that have been made as compared to last year's Estimates in the various documents I am tabling today and pertinent press releases, I would like to put this total increase into its proper perspective, namely, the economic environment in which we live and the effect of including in the Estimates some of the measures introduced by the Government last year.

We are all very much aware that the Canadian economy has been passing through one of the most difficult periods since the Second World War. While encouraging signs of improvement are beginning to emerge, particularly with regard to inflation and interest rates, we must be mindful that the recession has been deep and recovery will be gradual. As Members know, almost two-thirds of these budgetary Estimates are for statutory expenditures, thus of a non-discretionary nature. That is, they are based on continuing authority given by Acts of the current or previous Parliaments. These acts determine the basis whereby individuals, businesses, provincial and other Governments become entitled to receive federal funds, and in most cases the amount of money to be paid. I would like to speak briefly about just four of these payments which are directly, and particularly strongly, affected by current economic conditions.
First, public debt charges, which include the interest due and payable on outstanding debt as well as servicing costs and costs of issuing new debt. These costs, totalling $18.6 billion in 1983-1984, are $1.8 billion higher than the 1982-1983 Main Estimates level. This increase is attributable to the growth in total debt, partially offset by lower interest rates. A key factor in the rise in total debt is, of course, the very sharp decline in federal tax revenues as a result of the difficult economic circumstances.

Under the Established Programs Financing Act, 1977, the federal Government contributes to the financing of hospital insurance, medicare, extended health care and postsecondary education. The federal contribution consists of a combination of tax transfers and cash payments, the combined value of which grows with the total value of economic activity in Canada. If the tax transfer portion grows very slowly, the federal Government makes up the difference in increased direct cash payments. The depressed tax revenues which I just noted have caused a sharper rise in the cash portion of the federal payment under Established Programs Financing, which has increased $1.1 billion, or 21 per cent, to a total of $6.6 billion in the 1983-1984 Main Estimates.
As the Minister of Finance has also noted, we cannot expect a rapid recovery in our economy and the level of unemployment is of particular concern. While the Government has taken a number of measures to improve employment prospects, the unemployment outlook remains difficult. As a direct result these Main Estimates show a dramatic increase in the Government's contribution to Unemployment Insurance designed to reduce the financial burden on the unemployed. This year, $2.9 billion has been allocated to Unemployment Insurance, an increase of some $ 1.681 billion over the last fiscal year.
The final statutory payments I will mention are the federal contributions to the Provinces under the Canada Assistance Plan. The federal Government pays for 50 per cent of eligible provincial and municipal expenditures for assistance payments, welfare services and certain health services. We also cover one-half of the costs of child support services, such as foster care and daycare and a broad array of other family and social support services. During 1983-1984 it is estimated the federal Government will transfer $3.1 billion to continue these programs. This increase of $0.6 billion, or 21 per cent, over the 1982-1983 Main Estimates level is attributable in large measure to current economic conditions.
I noted earlier that the Government has taken a number of decisions in the past year not only to increase spending in existing programs to ease hardship and speed recovery, but has also implemented a number of new initiatives. Of course, since some of these initiatives were approved after the 1982-1983 Main Estimates were presented to Parliament, they have been funded through Supplementary Estimates in the current fiscal year.
I would like to mention just three of these items which are included in the Main Estimates for the first time in the 198384 documents which I have tabled today.
With the passage of legislation in June, 1982, the Petroleum Incentives Program became fully operational and the Supplementary Estimates (B) which I tabled last November included $1.8 billion for this item in the current fiscal year, 1982-83. These payments are included in the Main Estimates, for the First time in 1983-84, and account for $1.2 billion of the total change from 1982-83 Main Estimates.
Main Estimates, 1983-84
Another new measure is the Small Business Investment Grant Program designed to assist small and medium-sized businesses. This new program, announced in the June, 1982 budget, accounts for $0.2 billion of the over-all increase from the 1982-83 Main Estimates.
The last item that I want to mention is the $0.2 billion increase due to funds included in 1983-84 Main Estimates for the New Employment Expansion and Development Program.
[ Translation]
Madam Speaker, these are only a few of the many programs and activities mentioned in the White paper. In fact, the Main Estimates contain hundreds of further changes, on both the plus and the minus side. I would therefore invite Hon. Members, if they require further information on the subject, to consult Parts I, II and III which I am tabling today, as well as the additional information appearing in the press releases.

Finally, I would like to focus on one other element of the budgetary Main Estimates, which is the total operating and capital costs of all federal Departments and agencies. The Department of National Defence has total operating and capital costs in these Estimates of $7.8 billion, an increase of $0.8 billion from 1982-83. This increase is in keeping with the Government's commitment to NATO to sustain the increase in defence expenditures by 3 per cent annually in real terms. A significant part of the growth continues to be devoted to the reequipment and modernization of the Canadian Forces.
The total operating and capital expenditures of all other Departments and agencies is $12.8 billion in these Main Estimates. This cost of running the Government, up $1.1 billion from 1982-83, is increasing only about one-half as fast as total Main Estimates. The category of total spending has roughly only kept pace with inflation over the past six years, thus remaining constant in real terms, despite the growing number of new programs and increasing demands for federal Government services. This year, the share of these total operating and capital costs in budgetary Main Estimates is 15 per cent.
Of course, as I mentioned earlier, this area of spending has been particularly affected this year by the Government's six and five restraint program, since operating costs are in large measure accounted for by the salaries and wages of some 225,000 federal employees. As Members know, the salaries and wages of our employees have been limited as required by the Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act. In addition, in preparing the detailed departmental budgets for non-personnel operating costs presented in these Estimates, the Government has limited Departments and agencies to a maximum adjustment of 6 per cent for the effects of inflation.
Of course, the total increase in operating costs is above 6 per cent, since there are additional resources required to enable the Government to develop and implement new policies and programs and to meet the increasing demands for existing program services.

February 22, 1983
Main Estimates, 1983-84
In the same vein, restrictive adjustments have also been applied to annually authorized grants and contributions made to organizations outside the Government.
I would now like to say a few words about the growth in the Public Service as measured by the increase in the number of person-years. The Government believes that for 1983-84 it should keep the rate of growth of the Public Service in the 1 per cent range, despite the calls by many for expanding Government assistance. Therefore, the Treasury Board has informed Departments and agencies with large person-year requirements that their 1983-84 authorized person-year level is in fact lower in total by 0.2 per cent than the levels shown in the Blue Book. However, there was not time to reflect throughout the Main Estimates this decision to limit over-all growth to 1 per cent without significantly delaying the tabling date.
Therefore, the Main Estimates documents before the House indicate a 1983-84 total of 258,463 person-years for Departments and agencies whose personnel requirements are controlled by Treasury Board. This figure is 3,141 person-years, or 1.2 per cent, over the 1982-83 Main Estimates. However, I have just noted that the Treasury Board has already taken steps to reduce this to 1 per cent over-all growth. A large proportion of the over-all increase reflects short-term requirements for the implementation of recent Government initiatives, such as the NEED Program.
In reviewing the largest specific year-over-year increases, pressures for the provision of greater services to the public become even more apparent. The Canada Employment and Immigration Commission has increased by over 1,400 person-years. Besides the requirement of approximately 500 for the administration of the NEED Program, over 800 will be used to assist in the processing of claims for Unemployment Insurance. In the Department of Transport an additional 250 person-years will be used for regulatory activities related to air safety and the operation and maintenance of air navigation aids and facilities.
The RCMP requires an additional 343 person-years for law enforcement and demand-driven functions, such as provincial and municipal police agreements which are, of course, cost recoverable.
To conclude, I want to say as President of Treasury Board that I have set as a major priority the continuation of our policy of improving the management and efficiency of the federal Government. I am well aware of the difficulties of the task. However, I believe we can still further improve management in Government and the efficiency and effectiveness of Government as a whole. The consequences of the current economic situation pose difficulties for Government itself as well as for Canadians generally. But it has also produced a positive effect in making us demand the best from our systems, the best from our people and the best from ourselves.

Madam Speaker, my colleagues and I briefly reviewed these Estimates in a briefing session which commenced at noon. These Estimates,
which are massive, involve Part I and Part II, as set out by the Minister, together with 47 baby Blue Books. The Estimates disclose to the House and to the country an unconscionable amount of spending. They are expenditures that we as Members and our constituents cannot begin to fathom even if we were to work on them day after day.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) presented his demands to the House under the borrowing authority statute on February 17, he said that the spending for the next current year would increase by 9.6 per cent. That was a total, complete and fraudulent misrepresentation to the House. That misrepresentation was repeated this afternoon by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray). He knows better. One is supposed to compare oranges and oranges, not oranges and apples. The President of the Treasury Board is comparing what he has spent so far in this fiscal year and what he intends to spend by March 31 with the Estimates for next year, which are always much too low.
Let me compare what he has said in the House in prior years with what he is saying now. In 1982-83, the Government produced its Estimates. I am sure Members will remember Part I of the Government Expenditure Plan. That book says that the Government would spend approximately $76,300 million. However, it spent $81,150 million. If you compare it against other items you will find that the Minister spent nearly $7 billion over and above what he said he was going to spend a year ago. What we are comparing here, when he says that his expenses are increasing at 9.6 per cent, are last year's Main Estimates plus Supplementary A, Supplementary B and Supplementary C with this year's Main Estimates. But this year's Main Estimates do not include an anticipated $600 million loss in Canada Post. This year's Main Estimates do not include what we are told is going to be required to continue with the further bail-out of Canadair and de Havilland.
What do the Estimates really include? They include the minimum amount that the Government intends to spend. Last year it came back to the House for $7 billion dollars worth of Supplementaries. Indeed, it has not come back for all of its Supplementaries yet. Supplementary C, which we do not have before the House yet, is going to be $1,850,017,341, and that is also included in these Estimates. We have a spending plan by a Government gone crazy, we do not know where they are going. The Government says that it has covered the contingencies by providing a 7 per cent central reserve and a 3 per cent envelope reserve. But all previous history indicates that these reserves are just not so. The fact is that if we go back over the history of this Government since it took office on February 18, 1980 we find that its expenses for the year 1980-1981 increased over the previous year by 13 per cent. Its expenses for the year 1981-1982 increased over the previous year by 17.6 per cent. Its expenses this year increased over last year by 17.8 per cent. Where are we going? They say it is going to increase 9.6 per

speechtext:
I thought it would be important that we take a look at some of the spending items in the Blue Book that we have analyzed in the brief time we have had.
First of all, I thought we might compare various kinds of things that the Government does. I thought we would compare, for example, salaries and wages. We are under the six and five program for salaries and wages. The salaries and wages paid by the Government this year will increase 8.8 per cent. That is where six and five is. Other personnel expenses-I do not know what they are, but they are personnel expenses-are going to increase by 13.5 per cent. The Government spending on transportation and communications-and bear in mind that a big part of that is Bell Telephone expenses that are frozen at six and five-are going to increase by 16 per cent. I suppose that is the extra gasoline required, or whatever, for a new fleet of Challenger jets.
There is one figure that I want to give you that I cannot believe. The Government says that its propaganda expenses are going to go down by 1.6 per cent. Perhaps we can analyze that as we go through the Blue Book to find out if in fact the propaganda exercise will only go down by 1.6 per cent.
But that is the only thing that goes down. Professional services go up by 15.6 per cent; rentals go up by 15.6 per cent; the purchase and repair of machinery goes up by 45.1 per cent; utility expenses go up by 14 per cent; construction of buildings goes up by 13.6 per cent and the purchasing of furnishings and fixtures in buildings goes up by 22.8 per cent. We have been told that it is the cost of the debt that is running up this budgetary deficit. That only goes up by 11.8 per cent.
I think we could then compare the expenditures by Department. The Government has broken the budget down into envelopes, and we all want to know what is in the envelope. In the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Energy envelope, goes up by 14 per cent. The Economic Development
Main Estimates, 1983-84
envelope goes up by 25.6 per cent. The Social Affairs envelope goes up by 19.3 per cent. Justice and Legal Affairs goes up by 15.1 per cent. Fiscal arrangements goes up by 10.6 per cent. External Affairs goes up by 12.7 per cent.
The Minister in his statement said that Defence was going up by 12.9 per cent. Again he is giving us a wrong story. The fact is that it is only 11.3 per cent. The reason is that he cut his Defence expenditures last year and now he is restoring them. Comparing Main Estimates with Main Estimates shows that Defence spending goes up by only 11.3 per cent.
I am not going to go through all these and bore everyone completely. I want to say that there is only one Department, one envelope in the whole bunch, that really does not go up at all beyond the six and five guidelines, and that is the cost of running this place. We all know the proclivity to waste that we have here, but our expenditures in this Parliament are only going up by 5.1 per cent. That is within the guidelines. We know what is wasted here, we know because we are here. We know what we could cut back in this place if we really wanted to, yet our expenses only go up 5.1 per cent. Think of what we could cut back if we really worked at it in other Departments, in other envelopes of this Government.
We have advocated to this House that a serious study should be made on the Estimates to cut them back, to get back to where we should be, so we will not have to continue to go to the market and borrow and borrow and borrow. There is unbelievable fat in these Estimates. It can be cut back, and it is a challenge to the committees of this House of Commons to tackle these estimated expenditures and cut them back.
In that respect, if the President of the Treasury Board had any real intention of trimming the fat in Government, he would form a special committee of this House to supervise the cutting back of Estimates. He would say to Departments, "I do not care what you would like to do. Here is what you can afford, trim it to that". This is a Government totally out of control. Expenditures have gone up in the 17 per cent range two years in a row, back-to-back. They are likely to go up 17 per cent this year even though the Government says it will be 9.6 per cent. This Government is out of control.
If you look at inflation, you will notice that with this depression we have had a lowering of inflation rates. Today the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) indicated in this House that the seasonally-adjusted inflation rate over the last three months was 3.2 per cent. If that is the case, why should Government expenditures be three times the rate of inflation in their increase? Why should the cost of Government creep up three times the inflation rate? Do we really need a positive increase over inflation by 6.4 per cent? Do we need that much more Government in Canada, or does this Government want us to have that much more government? Is this the kind of Government that gets Chairman Mao to do its projections? That is what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) suggested.

February 22, 1983
Main Estimates, 1983-84
I suggest that if we allow this kind of expenditure program which is now set to go at a rate at least three times higher than what the Government says is the current inflation rate, we have done a great disservice to our constituents and to Canada. These Estimates are improper, wasteful and must be turned back.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this really is a "Gray Day" for Canada. We have just had the opportunity of perusing about three kilograms of "Gray" matter in an effort to understand what it was the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) was telling us a few days ago. At that time he said, "Just hold off, Canadians, because I promise you I am not going to say a single word of what will be in the $19 billion request I am bringing forward today, but just wait until February 22 because it will all be in the Estimates and you will have a very clear idea of what the Government of Canada is going to do with your money."
Something is drastically wrong. We have just had the opportunity, not to study carefully I admit, but to peruse the Estimates for the forthcoming year. Either there is a plan for the Government to do nothing particularly new other than simply lift all of the budgets up a number of percentage points, which I will come to in a moment, or the Minister of Finance was unintentionally misleading Members of Parliament and Canadians.
When you look at the documents before us, some very puzzling points come to mind. For example, I remember quite distinctly the Minister of Finance saying that Government expenditures this year will be up not 6 per cent, as the guidelines of the Government would indicate, but 9.6 per cent.
A lot of senior citizens in this country are puzzled because their increase was restricted to 6 per cent. A lot of mothers in this country were expecting a higher increase in their Family Allowance rather than having it capped at 6 per cent. The Government said it would ignore all their six and five programs and lift their expenditures by 9.6 per cent.
We talked to a number of officials from the Government who presumably are knowledgeable on how the Government plans to spend its money. They suggest that the budgetary Main Estimates for 1983 are going to go up 17.4 per cent. I think you can use some peculiar form of rationale, smoke and mirrors and some creative accounting to justify those two figures, 9.6 and 17.4. However, this document tells us that the Main Estimates, that area of Government expenditure where the Government has discretionary power, will increase more than 17 per cent in the coming year.
What does that say about the Government's attitude toward its six and five program? What does it say about the Government's attitude toward honesty, fair play and being forthright with the people of Canada? They say different things, depending on which Minister is making the comment. Whether that is intentional or not I leave up to people's speculation.
At this point one begins to wonder whether there is some effort being made on behalf of Government Members to encourage the public of Canada to think in creative ways
about what it is they are doing. Canadians were waiting for the Government to indicate today how it will be spending the taxpayers' money and borrowed money in the year ahead. They have waited to see what the Government plans to do.
I note with interest that the Government has given up forecasting. It has made so many errors in the last 12 months that any attempt to forecast for another year or more would be totally futile. It simply does not have the ability, the talent or the technology to make any real comment about where the economy is going. For that reason I say that these Estimates are virtually useless at this point.
The Estimates that have been tabled today will not help Members of Parliament, Canadians or anyone else to understand what the Government is trying to do, unless it is trying to do nothing. That they will understand. We cannot rely on the Estimates before us. Let me give a single example of that.
A gross distortion of information has been presented in the Estimates for the past year and for this year. I read with interest in one of the summary statements that direct job creation under CEIC was going to increase by $216 million. When we look at what actually happened, we find that expenditures did not increase by $216 million. As the Government's own forecaster suggested, they increased to approximately $482 million. That is a 125 per cent error in the Estimates. When you look carefully at what that means, not only was there a 125 per cent error in the Estimates of last year in that very critical area of job creation, but it will increase total job-creation expenditures for this fiscal year by only 21 per cent.
What kind of signal is that to the people of Canada? The Minister of Finance said that unemployment will be dramatically high this year, and that it is one of the highest priorities of this Government. However, when you look at what the Government is estimating for 1983 in the area of job-creation, you find that they are going to be expanding by only 21 per cent. The figures before us do not say that. They say that job creation will go up by 170 per cent. That looks good, a 170 per cent increase. However, when you look at the fine tuning, when you do the simple calculations, you find that it is not a 170 per cent but a 21 per cent increase. That is their commitment for real job creation in 1983?
One can only say, Mr. Speaker, just based on that one simple example-and we have not even begun to analyze these Estimates which are critical for 1983 job creation-that the Government is misleading the House in a dramatic way.
However, let us consider something else which we find in these Estimates, Mr. Speaker. I am assuming, first of all, that we all agree that job creation is important. We would like to see more money moved into that particular area. We find from the Estimates, then, in terms of direct job creation under CEIC,-that $100 million more than was spent last year will be invested in job creation. We also noticed that a certain amount of money has gone for PIP grants. Not $100 million,
February 22, 1983

Mr. Speaker, but $1.15 billion has gone for PIP grants to encourage, by and large, the multinational oil companies to explore the frontier areas of Canada. I am not making a judgment on whether or not that is a wise investment, but I personally do not think it is a particularly wise investment. But let us just say that $1.15 billion is going to assist, by and large, the multinational oil companies operating in Canada to explore in the frontier areas. How many jobs will that $1.5 billion create, Mr. Speaker? If we are seriously interested in job creation, that is the most unlikely place to spend a single dollar. The jobs created in that sector under the PIP grants will give us less return than spending money in any other sector of Government spending. Setting aside the rhetoric and looking at where the Government is actually going to be putting its job-creation money, Mr. Speaker, tells us that they are not serious when it comes to job creation because their actions go completely against the rhetoric which we hear from some of the more progressive Members opposite.
I notice with interest, as well, where some of the Government priorities lie, again without necessarily making a judgment at this point. I notice that when it comes to Government spending for operating and in capital costs, over-all Government spending by the Minister of Finance's own admission, is going to increase by 9.6 per cent. Let us say for a moment that we believe him. I personally do not believe him on this point, but if we take him at his word, he says spending for Government operating and capital costs will increase by 9.6 per cent. But there is another area, which is quite different from the 9.6 per cent area, and that is the area of Defence. Defence expenditures appear to be going up 11.3 per cent. It seems that in terms of over-all Government spending, we have identified military spending as a higher priority than other areas. That is an observation. I also notice something, Mr. Speaker, which I believe is a very sad comment on the Government's position towards war veterans. We realize as Members of Parliament how much time it takes to process concerns brought to our attention by veterans. Yet, in terms of person-years, one of the few Departments in the Government which is going to have a decrease of 11.4 per cent in person-years is the Department of Veterans Affairs. Some veterans in my constituency have waited one year, and some two years, simply to have their applications processed through to completion. To find that man-years in the Department of Veterans Affairs are going to be decreased by 11.4 per cent leaves one simply speechless.
We also notice, Mr. Speaker, there is no reference in these Estimates of Government expenditures for 1983 to de Havil-land and Canadair when they come back asking for $100 million each, or $200 million or $300 million. There is no mention of that, when those companies are on record themselves as saying, "We will be back asking for more when we require more." There is no mention of that, Mr. Speaker. There is also no mention of the contract work which the Government relies on to a large extent. There is an attempt, and 1 commend the Government for it, to evaluate carefully its expansion in terms of man-years to ensure that the return to the Government is maximized. But when I see there is no mention of money set aside for contract work, and knowing the amount of contract work which takes place, particularly with
Main Estimates, 1983-84
the federal Government, I believe we are leaving a large void, a large vacuum in these Estimates.
If the Government, and the Minister himself, are serious about these Estimates, when these Estimates go to the respective committees they should receive the kind of thorough analysis which they deserve, not the usual sit around and chitchat with the Minister for an hour or two, a handful of questions and a lot of gobbledygook on behalf of the Minister trying to skate around the issues. Then we vote, and the majority of the Government Members vote in favour and the Opposition vote against, and we all go home for the evening. That is not the kind of examination, study and investigation which Canadians want, Mr. Speaker, during these very critical times.
When we discuss those Estimates in the House of Commons or in committee, what is our goal? What is the point of these Estimates? What is the point of our discussion, our analysis, our examination? Are we attempting to find ways and means of developing a full employment option for this country? Are we trying to reduce Government spending by a certain amount? Are we attempting to support certain kinds of industries or provide certain kinds of services to Canadians? What is it, Mr. Speaker, that we are attempting to do with this examination? If we are simply examining it for the sake of examining it, then, of course, it is not going to be an appropriate investigation. Therefore, before we go into committees to examine these Estimates, surely we need to have some kind of strategy, some kind of game plan, some kind of program which will direct us in our inquiries to see if in fact we are getting the "bang for the buck" which Canadians ought to be receiving.
In conclusion then, Mr. Speaker, I make an appeal on behalf of the New Democratic Party to the Minister: when we have an opportunity to evaluate these Estimates in detail, as the Minister has indicated in his speech, would he give us a framework within which to operate, a strategy, so that our examination can be aimed toward some purpose, some goal, so that there is some objective which the examination is attempting to achieve.
We look forward to getting the Estimates into committee as quickly as possible. In attempting to digest these Estimates, however, Mr. Speaker, I think that a great deal of that enthusiasm and commitment to do the job well will be eliminated because we all know how successful these Estimates have been in years past at predicting and explaining the reality of the Canadian economy, and going in with that cloud over us, I suspect that once again this examination is going to be marginal, if not completely fruitless.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to the best of my knowledge, going back to the last time there was a statement on motions, I do not remember any correlation between the length of the Minister's remarks and the questions. I believe we can, on this occasion, agree to that, but I would much appreciate the question period being controlled by the Chair in accordance with the flow of questions and the sense of the House.
With all due respect, I would also ask that Your Honour monitor the answers on this historic occasion of the first statement on motions since December, 1981. I do not feel that this should be a precedent which is set in stone, for I want some time to think about this and discuss it with my colleagues.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would agree with the suggestion that rather than allocating a certain period of time, we should leave it to the discretion of the Chair to decide when a meaningful interchange of questions and answers has terminated. I know that the Minister himself, judging from his comments to us earlier and the thrust of his speech, is an individual who is open and quite prepared to do his best at this point, to examine and clarify any questions raised by Hon. Members.
In the spirit of the Minister's comments, I would suggest that rather than setting aside a prescribed period of time, let us just see, and perhaps after only ten minutes Your Honour might, in your wisdom, find that the ebb and flow is sufficient, or perhaps that it should continue for 30 minutes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House believe your proposition is a reasonable one. I might say that we are frequently urged by Hon. Members opposite to have more statements by Ministers. Quite frankly, I would think that would be a healthy trend, but it cannot be totally open-ended. There must be reasonable limits. I welcome Your Honour's proposition.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: I agree with the Parliamentary Secretary when he says it would be healthy for Parliament to have more statements on motions. With regard to the question as to whether or not there should be fixed times attached to the length of the question period, may I put forward at least one argument for Your Honour's consideration as to why that is probably better left to your discretion? If we state that the period will be 20 minutes, we will have then signalled to the Minister answering the questions how much time he needs to use up. He could have two questions and two ten-minute answers. He would then know he would have to work until 20 after.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Not Herb. Be fair.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: If it is left to Your Honour's discretion, then I believe the Minister would be more likely to be psychologically forced into the position of answering the questions that Hon. Members might ask. On the other hand, if he knows that all he must do is use up 20 minutes, then it is to his advantage. He would simply need to know how much time he has for buffoonery, without necessarily responding to the question. I think that if Your Honour believes it should be 20 minutes, Your Honour's judgment would be fine, but it should not be a preknown fact.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: The Chair thanks Hon. Members for their wise comments. Standing Orders do create some difficulty for the Chair in the proceedings inasmuch as they leave the matter entirely to the discretion of the Chair. I have made good note of Hon. Members' responses to the Chair's suggestion and I will be guided accordingly.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), dealing with some of the questions which have been raised by the two Hon. Members who spoke previously, and which we attempted to explore in the lock-up.
First, last year the Government forecast an increase in outlays of 11.7 per cent in the Main Estimates while, in actual fact, the increase in Government expenditures was 17.8 per cent. I believe my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), made that point. The Minister is now forecasting an increase in Government expenditures of 9.6 per cent. What assurances can the Minister give the House that he can hold Government outlays to 9.6 per cent in the absence of any budget or revenue forecast or, in fact, any responsible fiscal forecast?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we are discussing here is a comparison of the total outlays as announced to the House by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in his statement last week and as restated in Part I of the Estimates, amounting to $81,150,000,000 for 1982-83, with a forecast of total outlays for 1983-84, giving a projected increase in total outlays of 9.6 per cent.
However, there are some elements in the total outlays projected for 1983-84 which indicate why we basically are discussing a forecast. We cannot be totally certain what the demand will be on the Unemployment Insurance Fund. It may require more, but it will hopefully require even less than we have estimated we will have to provide.
With respect to our transfers to the Provinces under the Established Programs Financing legislation, we have estimated that our cash transfers to the Provinces will have to increase because the tax revenues which they had expected to receive under this legislation are likely to be less because of the weakened economic situation. This may also change.
Therefore, we are giving a picture at a point in time as to what we expect the total outlays for 1983-84 to be. But we are obviously discussing a forecast. We will work in order to stick to it, but there are certain factors not under our control which
February 22, 1983

will affect the amounts of money which we will have to provide under statutes passed by this Parliament.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address another question to the President of the Treasury Board. I can understand his problem in dealing with a forecast which is at a special moment in time. However, what I cannot understand is the difficulty which the Government seems to have on its side of the House in getting its own numbers together. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) has already discussed the discrepancy in the job program, and I would like to address one concerning the housing program.
The allocation for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation shows a substantial increase this year of about $482 million. In the Blue Book Estimates, the Government states that $122 million of this amount is included for the purposes of extending the Government aid program to first-time home buyers. In his statement last week, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) used the figure of $240 million. There is a discrepancy of $120 million in the space of a few days. Could the Minister explain why it is not possible to get better numbers on some of these spending programs?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: What's a million?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: What's a hundred million?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is the custom, when one deals with specific programs, to address the question to the Minister responsible. However, I would remind the Hon. Member that subsequent to the Main Estimates for 1982-83 which were tabled last year, we had the June budget and the October economic statement, and both of those declarations proposed to Parliament substantial additional expenditures in such areas as housing. The Hon. Member should take that fact into account when making her comparison with regard to numbers.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the President of the Treasury Board another question. I am not referring to figures which are tabled months after each other. I am referring to program figures or Estimates which are given in this House by the Government within days of each other, which indicate that the Government's financial figures given to us are unreliable, and not to be trusted.
According to the Privy Council Estimates, this year the Government will spend about $4 billion on commissions of inquiry, task forces and others.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Four billion?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: How much of this amount will be related to the Macdonald Commission on the economy?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Did the Hon. Member say $4 billion or $4 million?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
I said $4 billion, which is the figure in my notes, but I will have to check the Estimates.
Main Estimates, 1983-84

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Yes. I respectfully suggest that the Hon. Member check her numbers. I think that most of the amounts with respect to the Macdonald Commission on the economy will be dealt with in Supplementary Estimates. I will provide her with the information, hopefully during the course of this question period, with respect to what is in these Estimates on the Macdonald Commission.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister about the Government spending on propaganda this year. He will recall that on page 15 of the June budget paper last year it was set out that in fiscal years 1982-83 and 1983-84 there would be $15 million for each of those years cut from departmental publishing and advertising, for a total of $30 million.
In view of the fact that on page 1-48 of the Main Estimates under the heading "Information" the difference between 198283 and 1983-84 is only about $5.5 million, could the Minister tell us where the other $24.5 million is in cuts in propaganda as promised by the former Minister of Finance.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I reject the use of the word "propaganda". The Government is carrying out activities through advertisements to inform the public, in exactly same way the Conservative Government of Ontario and the Conservative Government of Alberta are doing. My hon. friend never complains about their activities which, in many ways, go beyond anything done by the federal Government.
I will be providing my hon. friend with further information in answer to his question. I can say that work is being done with respect to restraint of advertising expenditures which, if my efforts are successful, will go beyond what is in the Blue Book.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, these figures were included in the June budget under the former Minister of Finance. Is the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) now telling the House that he has not given the sort of attention that is necessary to these Government-wide figures on information, propaganda, advertising and publications-he can use his own terms? Is he saying that he has not bothered to check to see whether the $30 million promised in the June budget has been cut out and, if so, where is the other $24.5 million?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not only working to see that what was said in the June budget was carried out, I am working to see to what extent we can go beyond that. I hope that when this becomes more evident even my hon. friend will applaud these efforts.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray). In Table 5 on page 149 under the heading "All Other Expenditures", the 1983-84 Estimates show $7.5 billion, while the 1982-83 Estimates were $3.5 billion. That is an increase of 88 per cent, Mr. Speaker. Given that inflation is approximately 8.3 per cent, how does the Minister account for this serious increase?

February 22, 1983
Main Estimates, 1983-84

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a whole range of increases that are not connected with the rate of inflation, nor should they be. We are providing substantial additional funding in support of housing, and substantial additional funding in support of job creation, both directly through Government efforts and in support of the private sector. There are a number of items like that which I do not think, nor do I think the Canadian public believes, should be limited to an increase equal to the rate of inflation. If that were the case, we would not be responding to the additional needs and requirements caused by our difficult economic situation. This is the explanation my hon. friend is seeking.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is too bad that this could not be translated into jobs. As the former Minister of Public Works knows, his program was a failure.
In Table 5, under "Purchase, Repair and Upkeep", the 1983-84 Estimates are $1,056 billion, while the 1982 Estimates were $726 million. That is an increase of 45 per cent. Given the inflation figures that I have just quoted, could the Minister tell the House why there is such an increase?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, unfortunately the need to repair and maintain Government buildings and facilities is not linked to the rate of inflation. The rate at which things wear out or need to be repaired has something to do with the degree of actual use and normal maintenance requirements. I wish it were possible to limit these expenditures to the rate of inflation in some cases. I would ask my hon. friend what the facts are with respect to the need to carry out repairs and maintenance in order to effectively preserve these important assets belonging to the Canadian people. I think we have to deal with the reality which may or may not have anything to do with the rate of inflation.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister a question about VIA Rail. On page 29-82, Vote 80 I notice that the 1983-84 Estimates are for $755.4 million, while the
1981-82 Estimates were for $540,617 million. Last year there was a 20 per cent cutback in VIA Rail services in order to save $100 million. If you deduct the $100 million from the 1982-83 figure, it means the Government is now asking for $200 million more in these Estimates for VIA Rail, with a 20 per cent cutback.
To corroborate that, in Part I of the Blue Book at page 49, the Minister said:
In the Department of Transport, of the total 451 increase in person-years, 155 are required for regulatory activities related to air safety, 104 will be used for the operation and maintenance of air navigation aids and facilities, and 127 have been approved for the Marine Program for requirements such as search and rescue, improved vessel traffic management services and a transfer of responsibilities from the Department of Public Works.
Man-years for VIA Rail are not mentioned anywhere. Where will the $200 million be spent-will it be totally on administration?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could suggest that this quetion be referred to the responsible Minister, but I will try to assist my hon. friend by giving him the information that I have.
First of all-and I stand to be corrected-when it comes to man-years for VIA Rail, that is not part of the controlled person-years under the jurisdiction of the Treasury Board. In any event, my hon. friend may recall that we had Supplementary Estimates last year of $137.2 million in order to reflect more accurately the cost of providing rail passenger service.
What we are doing, basically, is to carry over to this year what was in last year's Main Estimates and what was in the Supplementary Estimates, with the exception of some additional funding provided last year for assistance to CN, CP and VIA employees who were affected by changes in railway passenger service.
The further increase of 1983-84 over forecast outlays of
1982-83, include $73 million additional payments for services provided by CP and CN, costed in accordance with the provision of the Canadian Transport Commission costing order R-6313 and the Commission's staff estimates of appropriate inflation indices for railway costs in 1983-84.
My hon. friend will recall that this is basically done after the fact, which is something that Members of the House have questioned from time to time. This matter is under review. I am also informed that the figures my hon. friend mentioned include the provision of $43 million for additional capital expenditures, of which the most significant item is further expenditure for the purchase of ten LRC train sets. This is a most useful support for Canadian industrial activity, especially since it involves something that the NDP spokesman claims to be interested in, and that is the use of significant Canadian technological development.
I hope this information will be of assistance to my hon. friend.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I stand to be corrected but I thought that several years ago we passed an Estimate which was a pay-out to CN, forgiving it for $600 million or $800 million so that it could operate on its own, as a Crown corporation ought to operate, and compete in the sector.
Is the Minister now saying that there is an extra $47 million in capital expenditures being given to VIA Rail in order to help it along, even though it is supposed to be running on its own? Did I understand him correctly as saying that some of that $200 million was designed as a kind of severance pay to employees who had been injured because of the cutback of 20 per cent of rail services?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again I think a detailed answer to this question should be given by the responsible Minister. I am told that there was funding provided in the Supplementary Estimates last year to assist in the adjustment of CN, CP and VIA Rail employees affected by the cutback in railway passenger services.
Again this is not a matter I claim to follow in depth or in detail, but I do not think either the House or the Government has taken a decision that VIA Rail is to be immediately selfsustaining. Instead, the decision of the House was that the
February 22, 1983

provision of railway services was a justified need and that, therefore, the House should provide payments to VIA Rail to enable that particular level of service to be maintained. This is why there was an amount in last year's Main Estimates that was approved by the House, and this is why there was a further amount approved by the House in the Supplementary Estimates. This is being picked up again in the Main Estimates for 1983-84. Of course it is up to the House to decide whether or not the amounts in question are to be approved.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a very short question for the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) dealing with the amount of money per job created in the area designated as PIP grants, with which the Minister is familiar. While I realize he may not have the figure available, will he give us some general indication as to what it would cost under that particular sector from a job-creation cost point of view?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that I do not have information about the cost per job likely to be created by PIP grants. 1 remind my Hon. friend that PIP was not intended to respond to the need for short-term job creation. Its purpose was to carry out a long-term and long-range program to develop our own Canadian oil and gas energy resources. It is part of a long-range effort by the Government, widely supported by the Canadian people, to develop self-sufficiency in oil and gas and to do so in a way which provides opportunities for Canadian industrial and regional benefits, both with respect to the provision of machinery and equipment and also jobs.
One has to look at PIP in a somewhat different way than one looks at the NEED Program, which was directly related to short-term job creation of a kind that, hopefully, will leave some lasting benefit. However, I do not think one would expect it to have exactly the same benefit from PIP and the results sought from it, in terms of creating a basically Canadian oil and gas industry in the hands of Canadians for the benefit of Canadians. PIP is a longer-term program.
While I will see what figures I can provide for my hon. friend in terms of job creation, I would say that this is a somewhat different matter from the type of jobs we hope to create and are creating under the NEED Program.
We are carrying out a long-term development of something which is basic to the well-being of our whole Canadian industrial base. It is reasonably well known that the oil and gas industry is not labour-intensive. Be that as it may, if it is not directly labour-intensive, it is still an outlet for Canadian professional services and, hopefully, for Canadian machinery and equipment. It is a basis for thousands of other jobs over the years in Canadian industrial sectors that will benefit from having a strong Canadian oil and gas sector. I think the Canadian public will, very much agree with the approach I have described.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, sometimes one wishes one had not asked questions which allowed the Minister to go off on so many tangents. I will try to be more specific in my last question.
Main Estimates, 1983-84
When we go into the respective committees to examine the Estimates in detail, does the Minister feel that there will be sufficient information to understand the priorities of the Government, so that we can evaluate the Estimates for particular areas within some framework and understand clearly what it is the Government of Canada is attempting to do today?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am told that there is no Parliament in the world which has so much information from the executive side of Government with respect to its expenditure programs. When one looks at the quantity of material which I tabled, it would be hard for any reasonable person to say that we are not making a very sincere and substantial effort to provide not only a lot of information but to provide information in a meaningful form.
I suppose it is always possible to bring about improvements. In fact, I said in my speech in the House that I intended to consult with Hon. Members as to how we could improve the format of Part II in the Blue Book. We have made some very substantial strides forward, not only in the quantity of information provided, but in its over-all quality.
I suppose we could go further. An effort was made to inform some Opposition spokespersons in the brief period available before I tabled the Estimates. If Hon. Members wanted to do their homework using the information provided, they would certainly be in a position to carry out a very meaningful investigation, not only of the Government's expenditure programs but of the priorities underlying them.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians have been deluged with bumper stickers and various advertising programs calling for six and five. The Minister has now admitted that the Main Estimates for 1983-84 will be up 9.6 per cent over 1982-83.
Will the Minister admit in good faith that once the Supple-mentaries are in, A, B, C and D, for the year 1983-84, the percentage increase will be closer to 17 per cent or 18 per cent, which will be a similar increase in terms of what Government expenditures have been in 1981 -82 over the year before and in 1982-83 over the year before?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am really not in a position to agree with my hon. friend. We certainly intend to make a very important and substantial effort to remain within the expenditure framework reflected by the total outlays figure. As I said to my hon. friend, there are certain factors which are not within the Government's control with respect to programs such as Unemployment Insurance and other statutory programs involving transfers to individuals, to businesses, and to provincial and municipal Governments. The Government is obliged to carry out what the statutes in question indicate. If because of a decline, for example, in revenues generated by the tax points allowed to a provincial Government, it is not getting the revenues it expected, the federal Government has no alternative but to increase the cash payments required under the established programs legislation.
If unemployment continues at high levels or even goes up higher-and I hope this never happens-the Government will

February 22, 1983
Main Estimates, 1983-84
be obliged to increase its payment to the Unemployment Insurance Fund. There are certain factors which we can forecast to the best of our ability but which are beyond our absolute control.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that of course is true, but from all the data which the Minister has and based on historical projections of the amount of the Supplementary Estimates, will he agree and admit that when we get to this time next year and look at 1984-85 the percentage increase this year over last year will likely again be in the order of 17 per cent or 18 per cent?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not prepared to agree or to admit that. Let us see what happens. Let us hope that things improve in the economy so that some of these forecasted expenditures do not have to be carried out at the level we have here. Perhaps they will be even less than 9.6 per cent. On the other hand, as I said to my hon. friend, you cannot say at this point that events will not develop so that we have to make payments above the forecast level. There is a possibility we will go above this. But we are giving a forecast at this point in time to the best of the information we have. All I can say is, let us see what happens, as the Hon. Member puts it, when we meet on this subject this time next year.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Order, please. The Chair, guided as it is by the wise comments made earlier at the beginning of question period, I proposes at this time to recognize two more Members who have risen; the Hon. subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray). I know it is difficult for him to answer questions that should be directed to appropriate Ministers, but in view of the fact he was recently Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and DREE, perhaps he could help me with the problem I have.
At the top of page 17 in Part I of the Estimates, funding continues for the organization of the pulp and paper industry. This troubles me because Canada had built one of the most modern steel industries in the world on the principle of capital cost allowance. If the steel industry can become modern in terms of world competition, why is that that the pulp and paper companies in certain parts of Canada have to rely on Government grants? Is it because they have been drawing down too much of their earnings in the form of dividends instead of using the money for capital replacement in order to remain modern, not requiring Government assistance?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that back, I think, in 1979 the federal Government and the provincial Governments of eastern Canada, including the Conservative Governments of Ontario, New Brunswick and those other Governments that were Conservative at the time, agreed with one another that it was in the over-all public interest, not only
in their region but in all of Canada to lever several billion dollars in additional investment from the private sector, the pulp and paper companies to enable them to modernize and upgrade so that employment would be stabilized and so they could meet competition from companies in the southern United States, where there are faster growing trees and totally new plants.
As a consequence, we have had the results we have been seeking from several hundred million dollars in joint investment by federal and provincial Governments. We have had investment by the private sector in modernizing our pulp and paper companies which will turn out to be several billion dollars. We have stabilized employment and we have made our industry in eastern Canada more competitive in a way that would not otherwise be the case. We have taken steps in the best interests of the entire country.
I invite my hon. friend to take this up with his colleagues, the Conservative Members of his caucus from New Brunswick, Ontario and Nova Scotia. They will give him the same explanation I have given him, and an even fuller one, if at all possible. They will strongly dissent from any suggestion by him that this program is not in the interests of their area or of the country as a whole.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot accept the answer of the President of the Treasury Board because it does not specifically address the question I asked.
I appreciate the need to modernize plants in those areas, but is it because the draw downs in dividends have been too heavy for companies to take advantage of capital cost allowance in the management of their balance sheet, as the steel industry has done and as other pulp and paper industries in Canada have done-as they have done on the West Coast? Why is it necessary for the Government to intervene where there has been less than good management, when the Government does not have to intervene where there has been good management?

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that I do not have any detailed information at hand that would be available to the Minister responsible for Forestry or to my successor, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley). The amounts are in the Estimates so that we can carry out our side of the agreements which were signed by Conservative and other provincial Governments with respect to the modernization of the pulp and paper sector of eastern Canada. Subject to correction when it comes to western Canada, we have provided assistance in other ways, marketing assistance through the COMDE Program. I could be mistaken, but we have provided assistance in some cases through the DREE Program in some of the Provinces. We have said that we are willing to sit down with the provincial Governments in Western Canada to see if we could develop a program equivalent to that already in place in eastern Canada.
I am not in a position to say what factors make the pulp and paper industry in eastern Canada differ from the steel industry, and so on, but I do know that if we had not done this we
February 22, 1983

would have imperilled, in fact lost, tens of thousands of jobs in areas represented by colleagues of the Hon. Member, and by his friend in his caucus.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Address the question, Herb.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: We would have failed to take steps that were strongly urged upon us by provincial Governments made up of the same Party he says he is a part of. The debate is not between myself and my hon. friend; the debate is as much or more between him and his colleagues in his Party from Eastern Canada. I hope those colleagues will note what he said and they will work it out in their caucus along with all the other things that they have to work out.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: We have no Gillespies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: You wish you did.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I will get answers from the Minister that will not get buried in that sort of political flim-flam in which he likes to indulge. I would refer the Minister to Table 2.1 and 2.2 of Part I of the Government expenditure plan. Along the same line as the point discussed by my colleague, the Hon. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I did not hurry to raise this because it is so rare that we get a ministerial statement in the House. I did not want to intervene in that process.
However, there was a matter arising out of question period which I think should be dealt with by this body because I
believe it deals with the ancient rights and privileges of Members of this House. My understanding of the basic tenets of the parliamentary process is that Members of Parliament oversee, review and pass Government policy into law, after some amendments, with regard to expenditures. As well, we review the Estimates that are based on the approval of those policies. We witnessed that function here this afternoon.
I noted that in the provincial legislatures of this country, a provincial Government introduces a policy to the legislature, the expenditures that are required to implement the policy are passed, and then the policy is put into place. I believe this is what happened with regard to provincial opposition to change in the Crowsnest rates.
We discovered today that some Provinces, having gone through that procedure, have received approval from provincial Members to embark upon an advertising program to oppose what is at the moment the Government policy proposal by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to meet that advertising thrust with an arbitrary action of his own. It is an action which does not have the backing or approval of the House. The policy has never been presented to the House. The Government is expending funds that have not been approved by the House since that policy has never been introduced in the House. We have no funds in last year's Estimates to embark upon a program of advertising to explain a policy which has never been introduced to this House, to explain why the Government may be coming in with a policy to do away with the Crowsnest pass rate agreement.
Therefore I submit that the expenditure is being made without the approval of this House. It has not been included in the Estimates of this House and, because it is being made without our approval, our rights and privileges as Members of Parliament are being trampled upon for many, many generations it has been the undisputed right and privilege of Parliamentarians to be presented with the revenue and expenditure proposals by the Government.

Money invested in housing produces real, durable products that respond to the fundamental needs of the Canadian people.
As the Minister of Finance has pointed out, it is not possible to relate the proposed borrowings to specific programs, but the need for additional borrowing arises from the extraordinary measures which the Government has undertaken to assist those most urgently in need of help and to continue and accelerate the economic recovery. Many of those extraordinary measures are related to housing. During 1982, the Government author-

ized a budget of over $1 billion to stimulate the housing industry.
I would like to remind Hon. Members of some of the highly successful initiatives the Government has introduced. To date, nearly 165,000 Canadian families have availed themselves of the $3,000 grant provided under the Canada Home Ownership Stimulation Plan to buy homes. That involved a commitment by the Government of almost half a billion dollars.
As Hon. Members are aware, the plan was extended to assist with the purchase of new homes built before the end of April 1983, and another $100 million was provided for this purpose. This program has had its intended effect.
I would like to remind Hon. Members that the number of single detached houses started in January 1983 across Canada was more than 4,800. This was the largest ever recorded for any January in Canadian history. Housing starts have rebounded to the level of 165,000, on an annual basis, in January. This sharp rise in production continues a trend which began in the last quarter of 1982, and I am confident that it is going to continue well into 1983.
At the moment our forecasters are talking about 150,000 starts in 1983. That would be a considerable improvement over the previous year. I would like to aim higher. I think, with interest rates staying low, chances are that we will be beyond the forecast level of 150,000.
Housing starts are not the only area where our efforts are being rewarded with success. As a matter of fact, as the Minister of Finance has pointed out, mortgage interest rates are now 12 per cent for one-year mortgages, the lowest level in several years. Six and five is working, and inflation rates have declined significantly. At the same time, $115 million has been established in grants for renovations under the Canada Home Renovation Plan. This program is very effective, creating jobs at a cost of $5,000 per person-year because of the way this program triggers private expenditure.
Under the Canada Rental Supply Plan, commitments were made in 1982 to provide interest-free loans for the construction of some 11,000 new rental housing units in communities where vacancy rates are low. There remains authority for an additional 19,000 units under this program.
I would like to point out that the effect of these very substantial investments by the Government are multiplied by the leverage which they exert on private money. Under the Canadian Home Renovation Plan, for instance, our experience shows that every Government dollar invested levers three more dollars of private money. The Government's contribution to date of $115 million represents a total investment of public and private funds amounting to about $450 million.
These Government housing initiatives have proved to be extremely successful, more successful than even our optimistic expectations. They have been most enthusiastically received by Canadians, which suggests that they are responding to a very generous genuine need. In this area, I wish to pay tribute to

my predecessor, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove), who brought most of these programs forward. These measures have increased public confidence in the home ownership market and made an important contribution to economic recovery and more employment.
While I am speaking of the strides we are making toward overcoming the current recession and improving the housing conditions of Canadians, I might draw to the attention of Hon. Members that the shortage of housing for rent that has plagued so many communities is very much improved. The latest Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation vacancy survey shows that almost 2.5 per cent of rental units were vacant as compared to about 1.5 per cent six months before. The forecast is that the vacancy rate will rise even higher in 1983 as more builders take advantage of the Canada Rental Supply Plan.
All the measures taken are designed to help restore the country's economic health and they make large demands on the Government's financial resources. The steps the Government has taken in housing have provided the basis for concerted national action to get housing moving again. The success of the Government measures has required the commitment and co-operation of other orders of Government, of the industry and of the lending institutions. We have worked together in a spirit of national purpose and commitment to get housing going and to contribute to economic renewal.
The Government's actions have demonstrated its concern for existing home owners, for first-time home buyers and for renters. Canadians see housing as central to their social and financial security, and our measures have helped restore that security. Confidence is needed if first-time home buyers are to purchase a house, and this confidence has been provided.
There are substantial rewards for the economy and for individual Canadians in achieving these results. A lot remains to be done, but federal housing actions in the past year will create an estimated 180,000 jobs. These jobs will be in rental construction, the construction of single family dwellings and the renovation and installation of existing homes. Jobs will be created in the production of building materials and in the manufacture and distribution of appliances and other household furnishings. These benefits will flow to all regions of this country.
The federal Government wants to increase the housing supply and its wants to restore security and confidence. The Government, through its actions, has provided over a billion dollars for housing initiatives. This is in addition to the Government's ongoing support for social housing, for rehabilitation under the RRAP, for home insulation and for support of native housing. These are new funds allocated to housing. It is important that Hon. Members and the public understand that these funds do not represent the replacement of private funds with federal funds. As I said earlier, many actions did trigger considerable investment of private funds in the housing sector. These funds provide incentives to Canadians.
