Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on Bill C-143. I suppose that while we are talking about that, I might say that there is an interesting ring for some Hon. Members in the numerals 143, because Members, such as the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger), the Hon. Member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga), the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski) or myself, when we leave this place to go home we take Flight 143. That, of course, is the flight into reality.
Bill C-143 is the flight-I am sorry the "fright" out of reality, and it is a frightful flight. That flight takes us down that frightful trail of $19 billion for most of which there is no budget. To say there is no budget is to say there is no plan. That means the Government is asking us for money to spend with no plan upon which to base its spending. What a frightful flight of reality it would be to grant that request of a Government with the record this Government has for spilling money or dropping it and kicking it away, letting it blow in the wind, trying to buy all kinds of projects which do not make sense, buying oil companies when the price of the company has doubled in value, but thinking it can have it. Nevertheless, the Government's answer is to ask for $19 billion without a budget to guide us to where it is going and to expect that Parliament, as the Minister said, would grant in haste the kind of request contained in the Bill, and to say also, "Trust us". That kind of trust is rather like not suspecting the tomcat when the canary is missing, because the Government's record is such that it is obviously suspect. We know that the Government is wasting the money of the Canadian people.
I want to spend some time today discussing how this institution began. 1 will not dwell on it, but I believe it is important. This House of Commons is called the House of Commons because it represents the common people. It started some 730 years ago with the Magna Carta. One of the principal reasons for the existence of this place, from the outflow of its history, was to control the King's purse. The entire revolt against the King in England was over wasteful spending, and because the King did not give justification for taxing his subjects. Today we find more and more that we are moving away from the notion that we are citizens of this country and adopting the motion that we are subjects of this country. We find it in our tax legislation.
The Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) raised the point that now our income is printed on the front of our tax forms. What the Government is doing is to reverse the presumption which had existed following Magna Carta, that Parliament, the House of Commons, was the place where common people went to represent their constituencies and to

control the purse. The presumption was that we had the right to the fruits of our labour and that some of it would be used for the general good of all.
Taxation is a fact of this century, not of 700 years ago. It is a new fact, but now the presumption is changing so that the Government says, "It is our money and we will allow you to retain some to build your homes, to run your farms, to carry on with your activities". The presumption is changing, which is demonstrated by the very fact that printed on those tax forms is information concerning the amount of money one earned, whether or not one was divorced, and one's social insurance number. We are creeping a long way away from the presumption of what the Government ought to be doing. It is important to realize that any Government which gives its presumption to the people recognizes the fact that its vested power is extended from the people. Power rests with the people. That is not the presumption today. The presumption today is that power rests with the Government. Government will make whatever decisions it wants, and be damned with the House of Commons and common people and common representation.
The Government's attitude is, "We matter, and only we matter. We will tell them whether or not they can bring their intentions before the House of Commons and whether or not they will tell them to the House of Commons itself'. Therefore, the notion of debating $19 billion, with no plan for its expenditure, should not surprise us. There is no budget before us. The Government simply wants the money. It wants to draw it away from the people. We are back to pre-Magna Carta times. We are back to the time when the King treated his people as subjects, not as citizens, when he had the notion that it was his right to raise whatever amount he wanted. It was King John who simply wanted to build a bigger castle and attack already overly suppressed people even more. That is the kind of Government we have today.
In speaking of property rights, let me say that in my constituency today many people think that what the subject of property rights concerns is whether or not they can keep their own farms or houses. That is not the question at all. That is an example to the question. What the question concerns is whether the individual has first prerogative to the fruits of his labour. That presumption has been changing in the last 15 years, under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The new presumption is that the Government has the first prerogative to the fruits of our labour, and it will leave for us that amount which it thinks we can have.

The Government has no budget, no plan and no projections. We have only heard the request, "We want more money". Well, who does not? Who amongst us does not want more money? Who in the country would not want more money? Who amongst us can go to a bank manager and say, "Sir, I would like some more money. I would like $1 million"? The bank manager would ask, "What would you use it for?" If the answer were, "That is my personal affair, sir, and I will not tell you", who would expect the banker to lend the $1 million?
However, the Government comes to us, to the public and says, "We want $19 billion".
I will tell Hon. Members how much $19 billion is. Some years ago the United States bought Alaska for $8 million. If the United States decided to buy Canada for $24 billion- although I will not put it up for sale because it is not within my power-that would amount to $1 million for every Canadian in the country. However, the Government wants to borrow $19 billion. Some people might become a little excited just over being offered $1 million and getting rid of the troups opposite, because they might see some better value in their country than this borrowing and borrowing year after year. I suggest to Your Honour that while the perspective is there, it is important.
We have a Government which does not even have the morals of an alley cat. It would give Donald Macdonald $800 a day to find out what the people already know, that we need less Government and more incentive for small business. We need to have less borrowing and less inflation. Donald Macdonald will tell them that after he has spent millions of dollars, when Canadians could have told them that for nothing.
Michael Pitfield gets reward upon reward upon reward, and then gets sent to the Senate. Judd Buchanan is allowed to build an apartment house where virtually no other Canadian could. What is his licence for that? It is just that he was a Liberal and was in the Government. Because he was the Minister who looked after parks, he got the advantage in the park.
Now we have the Gillespie situation which comes down to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) and the giving of gifts to those who give gifts in that inner circle. Canadians are certainly not at all pleased that their dollars are being spilled in this way. To borrow is to receive value today to be paid back at some future time.
Today we have a $140 billion debt on our future. That is the accumulated federal debt, and it will not be paid back tomorrow, next month, next year or in the next decade. A debt of that magnitude, if it is paid back at all, will be paid by the next generation. We have mortgaged our children before they are even born. We have mortgaged the next generation. We have put a price on the unborn. That is what is happening with this enormous debt. Through selfishness and greed the federal Government has been willing to put a price on the next generation. We have condemned our children, our resources and our country to the selfish pleasures of the "right now".
Last December this country went into debt to the tune of $300 million per day-every day Mr. Speaker-Saturday, Sunday, weekdays and Christmas day. That is a 300 per cent increase over the same month the previous year.
We have leeches that suck, through this Government-that cause the Government to impose extraordinary taxation upon us. Those leeches come in the form of 480 Crown corporations, the buying up of oil companies at double their value for some

foolish reason such as just saying they are ours. They are ours, but those debts are ours and those payments are ours. This debt-ridden Government is ours. We are living with every increasing Government expenditures. The Liberals have wasted their tomorrows in pursuit of the moment.
We need to compare ourselves with other countries, Mr. Speaker. Today, in the 22 Latin American countries there is a population of 360 million. Those countries have a combined debt of $300 billion. It is important to bear that in mind. Canadians understand that Latin America is in a very difficult financial position. The Canadian debt per capita is seven times larger than the per capita debt of the Latin American countries, however. Their population is 15 times that of Canada but their debt is only a little more than twice ours. The 24 million people in Canada have a $140 billion debt, while the 368 million people in Latin America have a $300 billion debt.
The only reason that Canada is not a Venezuela, a Mexico or a Brazil is that this country is resource strong. With this debt of $140 billion the Government has taxed those resources, has taxed our future and the children of tomorrow. That is a mortgage against the future that we should never allow. I repeat, per capita our debt is seven times more than that of the peoples of Latin America.
The richest nation in Latin America, Brazil, has a debt of $80 billion, less than ours, and it is teetering on the edge of bankruptcy. The only reason that we are not bankrupt is that we have the largest volume of fresh water in the world, the largest hard-rock mineral base in the world, and the largest amount of forest in the world. But we have mortgaged the future of our resources and our children.
The Government does not care how it manages the economy, Mr. Speaker; it only cares that it manages power. Power is the quest of the Liberals, not their achievement. If they can retain power, achievement is irrelevant. They simply want to hang on to the reins and continue to drive, without any regard for the potential of the men and women in this country who want to use their initiative to make the country grow. They want to believe that the country is ours because of their work. The Government wants to have control-to schackle and encircle people with bureaucracy.
In this country today the small business sector requires twice the secretarial staff, the number of lawyers and accountants, of the comparable small business sector in the United States. That is how much bureaucracy controls and directs our small business sector. We should recognize that the small business sector is the engine of our society.
The Liberals have requested the borrowing of $19 billion without any planning. It is now taxing without hope. It is a hopeless tax on hope itself-a tax on tomorrow, a tax on our future. They are borrowing against tomorrow's dreams simply to sustain their wasteful spending.

Mexico could not sustain its debt, Venezuela could not sustain its debt, Poland could not sustain its debt, and Brazil is teetering on the brink of bankruptcy. Money is not wealth. That fallacy was adopted by Mexico, Venezuela and Poland, but most particularly Mexico. In the belief that money was wealth, they printed more money and borrowed more money.
A recent article in The Economist pointed out that in one short period Mexico borrowed $80 billion but that it would have been a wealthier country today with more people employed and a greater industrial base, had it only borrowed $40 billion.
When you borrow, you borrow against tomorrow; you borrow today to have a new tax tomorrow because borrowing is a debt against the future. That is the way it is in Mexico. In this country we are in danger of running our resources into the ground. There is a risk that they will be for sale at wholesale prices tomorrow, simply to excuse us from our debt.
The currency would have been stronger in Mexico, had it borrowed less. Its foreign payments would have been less, it would have retained more of its domestic earnings and its unemployment rate would have been lower than it is now. Canada is following the example of Mexico. Borrowing dollars is not a creation of wealth.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-APPLICATION OF FEED FREIGHT ASSISTANCE PROGRAM TO MARITIME FARMERS. (B) DIVISION OF FUNDS BETWEEN QUEBEC AND NEW BRUNSWICK
AGRICULTURE-APPLICATION OF FEED FREIGHT ASSISTANCE PROGRAM TO MARITIME FARMERS. (B) DIVISION OF FUNDS BETWEEN QUEBEC AND NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 10 I put a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I presume that his Parliamentary Secretary or his designate is here this afternoon to respond. At the time, I raised the issue that the cost of feed grain in the Maritime region of Canada will be greatly increased due to the current proposed policy of the Government to do away with the Crow. I expressed concern of behalf of the farmers who felt that they would be adversely affected, and, indeed, are adversely affected, due to a reduction in the Crow rates.
Prairie farmers now pay approximately 18 per cent of the transportation costs of their feed grain, whereas in Truro, Nova Scotia, and in that part of the country, livestock producers and poultry producers are paying upwards of 75 per cent of the costs of their feed grain. Of course, it is very
difficult to compete under those circumstances and the Government proposal will make it that much more difficult in years to come.
The Government has recognized that the Maritime Provinces and New Brunswick in particular have a tremendous amount of agricultural property that has potential for the production of feed grain. As a result, it is looking forward to the time when New Brunswick as well as the rest of the nation will become self sufficient in the production of feed grains. However, the Government recognizes, and certainly the farmers in the region do, that this is a substantial distance down the road.
I asked the Minister if he would consider allowing the Feed Freight Assistance Program to remain in place in the meantime along the guidelines that were proposed by the Maritime Farmers Council in a recent brief to the Minister of Agriculture. They stated in that brief that all three provincial federations of agriculture and the Maritime Farmers Council have committed considerable effort toward developing a feed grain plan for the region. They believe that this new approach they are proposing would be fair and appropriate for all three Provinces and, indeed, would encourage a balanced development of Maritime agriculture.
The main points they were making to the Minister of Agriculture were; the restoration and future indexation of the level of support under the Feed Freight Assistance Program which prevailed in 1976; and the transformation of the FFA Program to a market and resource neutral system of direct feed cost equalization payment. When the Minister responded to that portion of my question, he stated as reported at page 22707 of Hansard:
We are very much aware of their concerns, but we think that a lot of them are unwarranted, for instance the increase in the price of grain.
That is precisely the point I was making. They are concerned about the increase in the price of grain. If the Minister of Agriculture were a farmer in that region, he would naturally be concerned, along with the rest of the farmers, because he would obviously not be in a position to compete with his counterparts in the Prairies and in the rest of Canada. I would ask the Parliamentary Secretary to direct himself specifically to that particular expression of concern expressed by these farmers.
My second concern on behalf of the farmers of the region is that the Government has earmarked $130 million to assist those regions, which are now not self-sufficient, in becoming self-sufficient in the growing of grain over the next five years. The Government has stated that it will give Quebec, which is semi self-sufficient in the production of feed grain, $90 million of the $130 million. It has earmarked $16 million for the Province of Ontario, which is completely self-sufficient in the production of feed grain. The Minister acknowledged this in his response to my question when he said in Hansard at page 22707:
-one will see that Ontario has a grain surplus producing area.
February 22, 1983

The Government will give New Brunswick, which is totally dependent on outside feed grain, $4 million over the same period of time to increase its feed grain production.
I would like the Parliamentary Secretary to please address himself to those specific points and tell the farmers of the region how it is that the Government has come up with those figures and what it will do to help tide them over until a period of time elapses and they become self-sufficient in feed grains.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Schroder (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-APPLICATION OF FEED FREIGHT ASSISTANCE PROGRAM TO MARITIME FARMERS. (B) DIVISION OF FUNDS BETWEEN QUEBEC AND NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as indicated by the Minister of Agriculture, feed grain prices in the Maritimes will not change because of this Government's decision to improve the grain transportation and handling system in Western Canada. The price of feed grain in Eastern Canada is determined by the cost of either U.S. or Ontario corn in Eastern Canada. Changes in freight rates in Western Canada will not influence the price of corn.
When freight rates for western grains increase, the net price that the western farmer receives for his grain delivered to a local primary elevator will be lower by the amount of the increase in freight rates. Thus a hypothetical $5 per tonne increase in freight rates on the Prairies will result in Prairie grain prices being lowered by $5 per tonne. In turn, the price of grain outside of the Prairies will not be affected.
The Feed Freight Assistance Program currently lowers the price of western feed grain by $10 to $18 per tonne on grain shipped to the Maritimes. Since its introduction during World War II, the Feed Freight Assistance Program has fostered the development of the livestock industry in the Maritime provinces. In fact, our Prairie brothers often complain that the Feed Freight Assistance Program and low freight rates for Prairie grain disadvantages Prairie livestock production, with livestock producers in the rest of Canada benefiting. Since the Feed Freight Assistance Program lowers feed grain prices in the Maritimes, it can work against the development of enhanced grain production there.
The Minister also received representations from the Maritimes to amend the Feed Freight Assistance Program to provide incentives for expanding local grain production.

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-CAPE BRETON COAL AGREEMENT- APPLICATION OF GUIDELINES ON MINISTERIAL CONDUCT. (B) KNOWLEDGE OF MINISTER OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
THE ADMINISTRATION-CAPE BRETON COAL AGREEMENT- APPLICATION OF GUIDELINES ON MINISTERIAL CONDUCT. (B) KNOWLEDGE OF MINISTER OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the last few days we have seen a dying Government lose every vestige of its claim that it is a moral administration.
The guidelines which require certain conduct of Ministers read in part as follows:
In any official dealings with former office holders, Ministers must ensure that they do not provide grounds, or the appearance of grounds, of improper influence, privileged access or preferential treatment.
It has been repeatedly suggested to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that at the very least there is a clear and unmistakable appearance of improper influence, privileged access and
Adjournment Debate
preferential treatment. We have a former Minister who makes a deal through his former Deputy, Mr. Cohen. How many people in Canada have ready access to the Deputy Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources? I suggest, not your ordinary person off the street.
Throughout negotiations, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources was heavily involved. Memorandums of agreement were signed between Petro-Canada and Mr. Gillespie. Mr. Gillespie appeared with the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) at a public gathering to announce this deal.
I think it is fair to say that many people would say that if a former office holder is dealing with a Government, Minister or a department for which he was once responsible, in a financial transaction, and is doing so before the expiration of his two-year prohibition period, as mentioned in the conflict of interest guidelines, that would give the appearance of improper influence and privileged access. Even Alastair Gillespie thinks that the ordinary person would get that impression. I quote a Canadian Press wire story of a few days ago:
Gillespie admits that outsiders-"ordinary people"-might believe his role as an energy minister and the experience he gained there, gave him a privilege or special advantage to get the development going.
Surely that is precisely why these guidelines were put in place. They are to prevent former office holders from doing business with the Departments or agencies for which they had responsibility within two years of leaving office. The reason is that to do so would give rise to at least an appearance of improper influence, privileged access and preferential treatment. Therefore, for a present Minister to involve himself with a former Minister is clearly a breach as well. This case is obviously a breach of the guidelines.
The Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister insist on avoiding the issue. They refuse to come clean with Parliament. The Deputy Prime Minister has even come to the extraordinary conclusion that these guidelines are merely tools which a Minister or former Minister may consider in shaping his or her judgment. To quote the Deputy Prime Minister:
These guidelines are self-enforcing. There is no monitoring agency. They are up to the conscience of the individual.
The sum total of what this means is that if in the mind of a particular Minister or former Minister the public interest is served, or perhaps the personal interest of one of the Minister's friends is served, these guidelines can be ignored. They are self-enforcing. Away with honour! Away with the notion that the Prime Minister has a responsibility to ensure that the guidelines are honoured! These guidelines are self-enforcing. The Minister's conscience is his guide. When we are given the Deputy Prime Minister's logic, when we are told he was guided by his own conscience when he dealt with Mr. Gillespie, it becomes more apparent how easily a breach of the guidelines occurred.
There is further evidence today that the project continues to exist only because of the presence of Mr. Gillespie and the

February 22, 1983

Adjournment Debate
cozy relationship he maintains with various Ministers of the Crown. And I say that, Mr. Speaker, because we have learned today that the great liquefaction project is of very dubious value from an economic point of view. A study within the Minister's own Department recommends that the project as currently conceived should not be supported by the federal Government. I quote:
Calculations made by the Department indicate that a capita! grant with a net present value of approximately $864 million in 1982 dollars would be required to raise the projected rate of return from 4.2 per cent to 21.4 per cent. Each permanent job created in Cape Breton would have to be valued at over one and one-quarter million dollars. From an energy point of view, the Scotia Coal Synfuels Project appears to be a high-cost source of synthetic fuels.
Those are not my words but words from the briefings and documents prepared by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. This deal not only appears to be a conflict, but most definitely is a conflict, and may very well be a bad deal on top of everything else.
These guidelines cannot be casually tossed aside by the Minister. I suggest that when the Prime Minister returns, he has the obligation to address the issue, make full disclosure of the facts in this matter and do the honourable thing, following parliamentary tradition.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-CANADIAN COUNCIL ON SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT POVERTY STATISTICS. (B) REQUEST FOR PENSION INCREASES
SOCIAL SECURITY-CANADIAN COUNCIL ON SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT POVERTY STATISTICS. (B) REQUEST FOR PENSION INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 9, amidst very loud shouting from Government backbenchers, I asked the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) to comment on the poverty statistics which had been released by the Canadian Council on Social Development, statistics which showed that 3.5 million Canadians were living in poverty in 1980. I estimated at least one million more people had become poor since 1980 as a result of direct Government policies, including high unemployment, part-time jobs, the imposition of six and five wage controls and the abandonment of a guaranteed income policy. I asked the Prime Minister to justify the increasing poverty which his economic policies had caused.
The Prime Minister shrugged off my question. He did not acknowledge or show serious concern for the increasing numbers of poor in this country, and he joined his Liberal

February 22, 1983

colleagues to laugh and joke about this. When, in frustration, 1 called him an uncaring millionaire, the Prime Minister refused to answer my supplementary question; an appeal to him to at least increase pensions to above the poverty line and provide some assistance for older women in their pre-pension years. His colleagues continued their disrupting uproar, which made it extremely difficult for me to be heard. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) indicated that the Government can do nothing to help.
The following day when my Leader again questioned the Prime Minister about his lack of concern and lack of programs to assist the poor of this country, he debated a theoretical poverty line, and I quote from page 22706 of Hansard which reads as follows:
That line is very much higher than it was several years ago. It is a moving line. It means that the people of Canada generally are getting richer. It means, since the average Canadian is getting richer, therefore the average poor person becomes poor at a higher level than he did ten years ago. So it is a conceptual notion which is debatable-
These ridiculous and uncaring responses to the most serious problem in Canada, and the frivolous attitude of Government Members who tried to deny my right to speak on this matter, are completely unacceptable to Canadians. It is no wonder the Government refuses to act when the Prime Minister is so totally out of touch with the real economic situation of so many Canadians, and when he obviously could care less.
The CCSD report entitled "Poverty Facts" provided statistics which showed that in 1980, 10 per cent of Canadian families lived in poverty. These statistics showed that 66 per cent of elderly women were poor, two thirds of all poor families were headed by women, 46 per cent of single women were poor and 20 per cent of families with two wage earners had poverty incomes. This was in 1980. How many more thousands are poor today? These figures did not include native populations suffering from extreme economic deprivation. Statistics are often as neutral as debatable poverty lines.
The Prime Minister should meet with mothers on welfare who are trying to raise their families on $400 or $500 per month. One mother with two sons had only $21 a week after the rent was paid to feed and clothe her family. She is typical. The increase in welfare roles alone should prove to the Prime Minister how desperate this situation has become. In my riding of Vancouver East, 12,000 people are on social assistance, and that is a 28 per cent increase over the past year. A single person in B.C. receives $375 a month, but only $144 in Quebec. There are many families and individuals in Vancouver East who are trying with great difficulty to survive on pensions and meagre savings. Hundreds of unemployed workers who could hardly live on UI benefits are now lining up at welfare offices and food banks, because their benefits are gone.
Women have always had the lowest incomes and for them the situation is worsening on all fronts. Yesterday the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women released a report which shows that women are more ghettoized than ever, with lower-paying jobs, while men are often paid twice as much for doing the same work. The NDP task force on older women,
Adjournment Debate
which held hearings in every province, found that women who are widowed or separated in their middle years and unable to work after a lifetime of homemaking are the forgotten poor. This group must be given priority, both in employment opportunities and income support.
The first step in doing something about poverty in Canada is to recognize that the problem exists and to try to empathize with those who are the victims. The Government must face up to the enormity of the problem and plan programs now which will help to alleviate suffering. Children must be a priority for action. Pension reform is urgent. Poor people in Canada cannot eat the unfulfilled promises of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. She must start planning now for the guaranteed income system which was promised over ten years ago. Poverty can only be solved by job creation programs and a positive strategy to bring about economic recovery, with incomes above the poverty line for all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Schroder (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-CANADIAN COUNCIL ON SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT POVERTY STATISTICS. (B) REQUEST FOR PENSION INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 8, 1983, the Canadian Council on Social Development released its most recent fact book on poverty. This publication and, more particularly, the press release which accompanied it, have resulted in a considerable amount of confusion as to the actual situation involving low income Canadians. I am pleased to have this opportunity today to address the issues raised by the CCSD.
First, I would like to address the issue of how poverty is to be defined and therefore measured. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated in the House on February 10, 1983, the choice of a particular line by which to measure poverty is in many ways arbitrary. Consequently, there are diverse views on how to define poverty. Moreover, these views may change from time to time, as evidenced by the periodic revisions which are made to the measures in use. Indeed, the Canadian Council on Social Development reflected a change in views by revising its poverty definition as explained in the fact book. Such a change in definition, however, does not mean that poverty has increased as indicated by the Council's press release. Rather, it simply reflects a change in view as to who is poor and who is not at a given point in time.
The large number of definitions currently in use confuses the real issue: that is, what is happening to poverty in Canada?
In its fact book, the CCSD quite clearly acknowledged that the incidence of poverty has been consistently declining since the 1960s. An examination of the table on page 7, for example, will show that, even using the Council's definition of poverty, the proportion of Canadian households in poverty in 1979, being 21.0 per cent, is less than it was in 1967, at 22.7 per cent. Moreover, the Council states again on page 7, that the reduction in household poverty over the period 1973 to 1979 is mostly attributable to the reduction of poverty among unattached individuals, mainly the elderly. This, of course, is the period in which this Government substantially increased the Guaranteed Income Supplement for elderly Canadians.

February 22, 1983
Adjournment Debate
The Council's statement in its press release, that the rate of family poverty now shows every sign of increasing, is not substantiated by the facts available to date, particularly those in its own fact book. This Government has made substantial progress over the past decade in reducing poverty, and is continuing to provide for the needs of Canada's poor as
evidenced by the special provisions of the six and five program to protect the benefits of low-income families and the elderly.
